entry.title: Re: SAP Sales Service Cloud Version 2 - Using external hook communicating with Mendix
entry.content:
Hi Adnan,

Thanks for sharing the headers. The relevant difference is Content-Encoding: gzip in the Mendix response (and no Content-Length, so probably chunked), while Node.js returns a plain body of 4413 bytes. This would also explain why {"noChanges": true} works: a tiny body is usually not compressed, while the full one is. The 2.39 KB shown by Postman looks like your 4.4 KB body after gzip.

My hypothesis, which I have not been able to confirm, is that the hook client in V2 does not decompress the response, so it cannot parse it. The Content-Type spacing difference is most likely irrelevant.

To check it:

  1. Call the Mendix endpoint with curl in three ways: no extra headers, -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" and -H "Accept-Encoding: identity". See whether and when it returns Content-Encoding: gzip.
  2. Test a response of about 1 KB to find the size where the failure starts (return only extension fields, which is also what a post-hook is meant to change).

If it is confirmed, options would be to avoid compression for this endpoint (check with Mendix whether the Cloud nginx compression can be disabled or excluded for that path), reduce the payload below the compression threshold, or place a small proxy in front (for example Cloud Integration or API Management) that returns the body uncompressed.

If you can confirm the result of the curl tests, we can narrow it down further. And if it is a gzip handling limitation in the hook client, it would be worth raising it with SAP, quoting the log ID.

entry.title: SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2:Setting Up Principal Propagation with OAuth2SAMLBearer Authentication
entry.content:
This is my 350th blog post, and I'm excited to continue sharing insights, experiences, and lessons learned with the community.

Introduction

When integrating SAP BTP services with SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 or SAP Service Cloud Version 2 or ESM, one of the most common requirements is ensuring that the identity of the logged-in user flows seamlessly from the source BTP application into the target SAP Cloud system. This is known as Principal Propagation.

Without principal propagation, every API call would authenticate as a technical/service user — losing all user context, audit trails, and authorization logic that depends on who is actually logged in. With it, the end user's identity is securely carried through, enabling fine-grained access control and meaningful audit logs on the SAP Sales/Service Cloud side.

This blog walks you through the complete setup using the OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion Flow — the recommended approach for BTP-to-SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 connectivity.

How It Works — The Big Picture

User (logged into BTP app)
        │
        ▼
BTP Destination (OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion)
        │  ── Generates a SAML assertion carrying the user's identity
        ▼
SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 Token Service
        │  ── Validates the assertion against the trusted certificate
        ▼
Returns an OAuth2 Access Token (scoped to that user)
        │
        ▼
API Call executed as the propagated user
The trust between BTP and SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 is established by registering BTP's X.509 certificate as a trusted issuer inside the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 tenant.

Prerequisites

  • Access to your SAP BTP Cockpit (subaccount level)
  • Admin access to your SAP Sales Cloud V2 / Service Cloud V2 tenant
  • Ability to call REST APIs on the tenant (e.g., via Postman, Bruno, or curl)

Step 1: Download the BTP Trust Certificate

  1. Log in to the SAP BTP Cockpit and navigate to your subaccount.
  2. Go to Connectivity → Destinations → Download Trust (top-right area of the Destinations page).
  3. A .pem certificate file will be downloaded.
  4. Open the file and copy only the certificate content — the block between (but not including) the header and footer lines:

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIIEXzCCA0...   ← copy everything between these lines
-----END CERTIFICATE-----

Keep this certificate value handy — you'll need it in the next step.

Step 2: Configure Inbound OAuth2 Trust in SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2

SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 needs to know about BTP as a trusted SAML assertion issuer. This is done via a dedicated IAM Service REST API on your tenant.

Important restriction: Only one OAuth2 SAML Bearer Inbound Configuration can exist per tenant.

2a. Check if a Configuration Already Exists

Send a GET request to check the current state:

GET <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration
  • If a configuration exists with the same BTP certificate → you can reuse it as-is.
  • If a configuration exists with a different certificate → update it (Step 2b).
  • If no configuration exists → create a new one (Step 2c).

2b. Update an Existing Configuration (PUT)

PUT <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration/<id>
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "id": "<existing Id found in Step 2a>",
    "clientAppName": "<A meaningful name, e.g. BTP-SalesCloud-Trust>",
    "certificate": "<Certificate content from Step 1>"
}

2c. Create a New Configuration (POST)

POST <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "id": "<BTP Subaccount UUID (This is to easily identify or you can provide your own UUID v4 format>",
    "clientAppName": "<A meaningful name, e.g. BTP-SalesCloud-Trust>",
    "certificate": "<Certificate content from Step 1>"
}

2d. Save the Response Values

A successful POST or PUT returns a JSON response like this:

{
  "value": {
    "id": "...",
    "grantType": "SAML2_BEARER",
    "nameIdType": "EMAIL",
    "spEntityId": "...",
    "audience": "<AUDIENCE>",
    "tokenServiceUrl": "<TOKEN_URL>",
    "clientId": "<CLIENT_ID>",
    "scopes": ["<SCOPE_ID>"],
    "clientAppName": "...",
    "certificate": "..."
  }
}

Note down these four values — you'll need them in Step 3:

Field Used As

audienceAudience in BTP destination
tokenServiceUrlToken Service URL in BTP destination
clientId → appears as CLIENT_IDClient Key in BTP destination
scopes[0] → SCOPE_IDScope in BTP destination

Step 3: Create the BTP Destination

Now configure a destination in your BTP subaccount that uses the inbound configuration values you just collected.

  1. Go to SAP BTP Cockpit → Subaccount → Connectivity → Destinations → New Destination.
  2. Fill in the following fields:

Property Value

NameYour choice (e.g., SalesCloudV2_PrincipalProp)
TypeHTTP
URL<Your SAP Sales/Service Cloud Tenant Host URL>
AuthenticationOAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
Audience<AUDIENCE> from the inbound config response
AuthnContextClassRefurn:none
Client Key<CLIENT_ID> from the inbound config response
Token Service URL<TOKEN_URL> from the inbound config response
Scope<SCOPE_ID> from the inbound config response
nameIdFormaturn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress

The nameIdFormat value tells the system to use the user's email address as the SAML NameID — this is how the user identity is matched on the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 or ESM side.

Step 4: Configure Trusted Domains in SAP BTP Authorization & Trust Management

As a final step, ensure that your SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 tenant domain is registered as a trusted domain in SAP BTP's Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA/SAP Cloud Identity Services).

Refer to the official SAP documentation: Configure Trusted Domains for SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service.

This ensures that SAML assertions issued by BTP are only accepted by explicitly trusted target systems — an important security boundary.

Summary

Here's a quick recap of the end-to-end setup:

Step 1 → Download BTP X.509 Trust Certificate
Step 2 → Register certificate as Inbound OAuth2 Config on SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2
Step 3 → Create OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion Destination in BTP using response values
Step 4 → Register SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 domain as trusted in BTP Auth & Trust

Once complete, any BTP application or service using this destination will automatically propagate the logged-in user's identity to SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 — without requiring users to re-authenticate or sharing technical credentials.

Key Takeaways

  • Principal Propagation bridges the identity gap between BTP and SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2, preserving the real user context across systems.
  • The trust is certificate-based — BTP's signing certificate is registered directly in the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 IAM service.
  • The fixed UUID (34f8b9d2-78c2-4617-bcf2-6eb36403c667) is a well-known system identifier for this configuration — don't change it.
  • Only one inbound configuration is allowed per tenant, so manage it carefully across teams.
  • User matching relies on email address as the SAML NameID — ensure users exist with the same email in both systems.

Share to your colleagues or Have questions or ran into issues during the setup? Drop them in the comments below.

entry.title: From Forecast to Flow: How Agentic AI Is Closing the Supply Chain Planning to Execution Gap
entry.content:
Most supply chains can tell you what is likely to happen. Fewer can do anything about it fast enough. 

Disruption is a big reason why. According to a Gartner survey conducted in 2024, 73% of companies surveyed have made supply chain network changes in the past two years. Considering continuous disruptions, improving resilience, enhancing flexibility and increasing agility are top of mind for Chief Supply Chain Officers (CSCOs) . In this kind of environment, a good forecast only helps if the organization can act on it quickly. 

Three themes stand out when you look at how companies are dealing with this: 

  • The gap is not the forecast. It sits between what planning systems know and what the supply chain actually does. 
  • Agentic AI shifts planning from recommending to acting. It works within boundaries that people define. 
  • Readiness is mostly organizational. Business rules, data, and trust matter more than technology itself. 

The Gap Between Forecast and Action

Forecasting has long been the centrepiece of planning, and for good reason. Get the forecast right, and the rest of the supply chain has a fighting chance. But better forecasts haven't closed the gap on their own. In many companies, the planning system already produces good output, and it still never turns into action. Planners override the plan because they don't trust the numbers, or because the inputs feeding the system were wrong, so the good output never reaches the decision. 

That makes this less of a technology problem and more of a confidence and execution problem. Speed makes it worse. Monthly planning cycles and batch-updated models weren't built for conditions that change this fast, and the result is a widening gap between what planning systems know and what supply chains are able to do with that knowledge. 

From Recommendation to Resolution 

AI has been part of supply chain planning for years, mostly as better forecasting models and dashboards that flag exceptions. The gains are real. McKinsey found that forecasting errors often fall by 30 to 50% when AI and machine learning are used in demand planning. But better predictions, on their own, don't move goods. These tools observe and recommend, while agentic AI is built to pursue goals, run multi-step workflows, and act within governed boundaries without needing human approval at every step. In supply chain terms, an agent doesn't just flag a shortage. It checks the downstream impact, models mitigation scenarios, starts a supplier reorder, adjusts production sequencing, and reroutes in-transit inventory, all in roughly the time it used to take a planner to open a ticket. 

This isn't a distant idea. Gartner expects supply chain software with agentic AI capabilities to grow from under $2 billion in 2025 to $53 billion by 2030 and predicts that 50% of cross-functional supply chain management solutions will use intelligent agents to execute decisions autonomously in that same window. 

The biggest value shows up in end-to-end orchestration. Isolated agents, however capable, can't deliver the coordinated response that today's volatility demands. What works is a demand agent, a supply agent, and an execution agent moving together, much faster than any human handoff could. 

What Companies Need to Get Right First 

The shift is organizational as much as technical. A few things need to be in place before agents can do their job. 

  • A faster planning rhythm. The traditional monthly S&OP cycle is already breaking under volatility, and some companies take two months to decide on an issue they raised. Many have added a weekly Sales and Operations Execution (S&OE) process, but that means demand, supply, procurement, production, and quality all need to show up prepared, with the numbers right, every week. A lot of teams end up building off-system Excel workarounds just to get there, which is exactly the kind of high-friction task agents are well suited to take on. 
  • Clear business rules. Think of onboarding an agent the way you would onboard a new planner. In a room of 60 supply chain professionals at a recent conference, nobody could say they had a written rule for how to prioritize customers during a shortage. If a human team can't state the rule, an agent can't be told to follow it. 
  • Data readiness. Agents working in near real time need clean, connected, timely data. Most planning data today is fragmented, refreshed in batches, and inconsistent at the level where agents need to act. 

Perspectives from Implement Consulting Group and SAP

Two Industry experts who work on this topic every day, Søren Skjødt of Implement Consulting Group (also referred to as Implement) and Philippe Wolff of SAP, shared where they see the value and where to start. 

Søren sees the barrier as governance more than technology. “The technology is ready and what isn't always ready is the organization around it”, he says.  

  • One of the best early wins is helping planners with the thousand small decisions that eat up their day, with an agent pointing out where action is genuinely needed before a human even opens the system.  
  • He cites a real-world scenario where an agent was trained to prepare for the weekly sales & operation planning meeting. The agent reviews signals across multiple systems and, when it spots a supply issue, pulls in customer context from the CRM, so the full picture is ready before the meeting starts. Cutting even one or two days of prep from a weekly cycle means better decisions, earlier, and it doesn’t need a major infrastructure overhaul. 

"How can we get an agent to prioritize for us if we cannot tell the priority? We need to have clear business rules, because these are the instructions we give to the agent." 

Søren Skjødt, Supply Chain Planning Lead, Implement Consulting Group 

Philippe sees agentic value in supply chain planning around three areas, each building on the last.  

  • The first is execution over planning: managing short-term exceptions far faster, which can compress a multi-day process into hours and is where the ROI is clearest.  
  • The second is post-planning intelligence: understanding why plans deviate from execution, such as lead times that keep running longer than the planning model assumes, so each planning cycle improves on the one before.  
  • The third is continuous planning, replanning on a rolling basis instead of waiting for the monthly cycle 

He advises starting on the execution side, where use cases are bounded, while keeping a clear picture of the end goal. 

"Define your North Star, where do you want to go, and how do you get to true autonomous planning? But already start the journey by implementing use cases where you know the biggest value is." 

Philippe Wolff, Supply Chain Planning, Global Domain Advisory Lead at SAP 

Conclusion 

The path from forecast to flow isn't a single technology rollout. It's a series of deliberate choices about which decisions to automate, which business rules to write down, and what data foundations to build. Companies don't need all of it figured out before they start. They need a clear destination, a governed first step, and the leadership commitment to see it through. 

Agentic AI doesn't replace the judgment of experienced supply chain professionals. It removes the friction that keeps that judgment from reaching the decision at the point it matters the most. 

Learn More 

To hear the full conversation with Philippe Wolff and Søren Skjødt, watch Episode 1 of the Agent Shift LinkedIn Live series that focusses on the increasing role of Agentic AI in Supply Chain Management.

entry.title: V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 4): Calculating the availability bonus in Convergent Invoicing
entry.content:
Introduction

In the previous chapters of this series, we explored how a Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) meter-to-cash process can be implemented entirely within SAP IS-U, including the calculation of an availability bonus based on the time a vehicle remains connected to the grid during discharging.

In this final chapter, I would like to explore an alternative approach: leveraging SAP Convergent Invoicing (CI) to calculate the availability bonus while keeping the conventional IS-U metering and billing setup unchanged. Instead of introducing additional configurations in IS-U to register meter-reading results in minutes (MIN), we can use CI to calculate the availability bonus based on the number of hours for which the vehicle was connected to the grid.

Meanwhile, the charging and discharging quantities continue to be registered through a conventional bidirectional meter in kilowatt-hours (kWh).

In other words, our IS-U installation requires only the conventional bidirectional-meter setup for the Meter-to-Cash process.

Bidirectional meter ISU_WALLBOX01 installed in installation 4100000514.

MR-results for charging and discharging registered in kWh.

Billing document 100000005601 – No amount calculated for availability bonus.

The availability bonus will be calculated separately in CI and subsequently integrated into the IS-U invoicing process. But how can we bring these two billing streams together and ensure that the customer receives a single invoice covering both the energy-related charges and the availability bonus?

Let's explore the required configuration and processing steps, from creating and rating consumption items in CI to joint invoicing and the resulting FI-CA postings.

 

1. Consumption Item Class (CIC) and Billable Item Class (BIC) creation

The first step is to configure a new Consumption Item Class (CIC). As a demonstration for this blog, I created a new CIC named “ZV2G”, specifically for the V2G solution.

Customizing path:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Basic Functions >> Consumption Items >> Consumption Item classes >> Maintain Consumption Item Classes

Consumption Item class ZV2G

Consumption Item class ZV2G – Interface components.

Once the CIC has been created and its interface generated, the system creates a corresponding database table. In this example, the generated table is /1FC/0ZV2G400.

Consumption Item class ZV2G generated database table - /1FC/0ZV2G400.

This table stores the consumption items belonging to the class, including items created for testing and simulation. After rating, the corresponding rating results can be examined in the relevant records.

Examples of entries created after simulation runs.

Once the consumption items (CIT) have been rated, the system generates the resulting billable items, which can be processed further in Convergent Invoicing through billing execution. For this scenario, however, I also configured integrated billing, which allows the billing document to be created as part of the rating process in my setup.

To support the V2G integration, I created a corresponding Billable Item Class (BIC), also named ZV2G.

Customizing path:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Basic Functions >> Billable Items >> Billable Item classes >> Maintain Billable Item Classes

Billable Item class ZV2G.

Billable Item class ZV2G – Database table /1FE/0ZV2G4IT00.

Billable Item class ZV2G – interface components.

It is important to note that this V2G blog post does not aim to explain every aspect of CIC and BIC configuration. The exact configuration depends on the intended integration scenario, the selected interface components, and the requirements of the implementation.

However, for a more detailed introduction to Convergent Invoicing and its integration with Utilities, I highly recommend the blog series by Oleh Korolyk, beginning with his article:

SAP Billing and Revenue Innovation Management: commodity and non-commodity services on one (or separate) invoice is no longer a dream

The article provides an excellent starting point and contains all the links to all other posts in his series.

I highly recommend reading this blog series as well!

2. Pricing and Rating Configurations

As discussed in the previous chapter, the availability bonus in our example is calculated using a price of −0.24 per hour (HR).

To implement this calculation in Convergent invoicing, I configured a pricing procedure for the relevant posting area 8200. This can be done by following the customizing path below:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Basic Functions >> Pricing >> Assigning Pricing schemas

For this example, I used pricing procedure CI1001, which is an SD pricing procedure that can be maintained using transaction V/08. A pricing procedure defines the sequence of condition types and calculation steps used to determine the applicable price.

Pricing procedures CI1001 with the condition types configured in its steps.

For this example, I used condition type PST0 to maintain the price applied when rating the consumption items. The condition record can be maintained using transaction VK11, with the relevant combination of sales organization, distribution channel, customer, material, and price unit, according to the condition type configuration.

Price condition within condition type PST0.

Configurations of material EXTM – Transaction MM03.

Once the SD pricing configuration is complete, we must ensure that the relevant pricing logic is executed when the consumption items are rated.

 For this purpose, I assigned the function module ‘FKK_BIX_RATING_EVENT_30_SD’ in the program extensions of the newly created rating group RV2G.

Customizing path:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Rating >> Define Rating Groups

I then assigned our newly created Consumption Item Class ZV2G to the rating group RV2G:

Customizing path:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Rating >> Assign Consumption Item Classes to Rating Groups

With these settings in place, the consumption items can be rated using the configured pricing logic.

The negative price represents the customer credit in this example. The resulting amount must be verified against the actual pricing and posting configuration to ensure that the availability bonus is represented correctly in the subsequent billing and FI-CA documents.

3. Provider contract for the availability bonus

After completing the required CI configuration, we can create the provider contract for the relevant business partner. For this purpose, I used transaction FP_VT1.

The provider contract must contain the relevant account and commercial assignments required by the pricing and rating configuration. In this example, these include the business partner, contract account, company code, sales organization, distribution channel, and material.

Provider contract V2G_AVLB – General Data.

The provider contract V2G_AVLB is linked to contract account 200000003200.

Provider contract V2G_AVLB – General Data: Linked to contract account 200000003200.

In the account assignment data, the provider contract is linked to sales organization 2510, company code BCMP, and product EXTM.

Provider contract V2G_AVLB – Account Assignment: Linked to Sales org. 2510; Company code BCMP and Product EXTM (MM).

These assignments allow the consumption items to be associated with the relevant customer account and commercial data used for pricing.

4. Creation and Rating of Consumption Items

Once the provider contract has been created, we can create a consumption item using transaction FKKBIXCIT_CWB.

 For this demonstration, I created the consumption item manually and linked it to the provider contract. The following information can then be specified:

  • Consumption date
  • Unit of measurement (UoM)
  • Quantity consumed
  • Consumption item type

The unit of measurement (UoM) specified in the consumption item must be compatible with the pricing configuration. Since our availability bonus is calculated per hour, I used HR as the unit of measurement.

Consumption Item 2608230005000000600001

In this example, we create the consumption items manually. In a production environment, however, consumption items would typically be created automatically from data received from an external application. For example, a charging station provider could supply the connection duration of a vehicle through an integration interface.

The interface would need to transform and validate the incoming data before creating the corresponding consumption items in your SAP S/4HANA system.

SAP provides APIs for creating consumption items. The exact API to use depends on the interface generated for the consumption item class and the SAP release. For the ZV2G class, the generated interface and its supported usage should be verified before implementation.

One option would be the general API ‘FKK_BIX_CIT_CREATE_API ‘:

Function Module FKK_BIX_CIT_CREATE_API in which function ‘FKK_BIX_CIT_CREATE’ is called.

Alternatively, SAP can generate a class-specific RFC function module for each Consumption Item Class, following the naming convention /1FC/XXX_CIT_CREATE_API. These generated interfaces are adapted to the structure of the corresponding class.

For our example, after generating the interfaces for CIC ZV2G, the system created the Function Module ‘/1FC/ZV2G_CIT_CREATE_API’, which is tailored to the structure of CIC ZV2G.

Function Module /1FC/ZV2G_CIT_CREATE_API adapted to the structure of CIC ZV2G.

Once the Consumption Item has been created, we can execute rating.

After successful rating, the consumption item receives the corresponding rated status:

Consumption item 2608230005000000600001 with status “Rated”.

In a conventional CI process, rating produces billable items that are subsequently processed during billing. As mentioned before, in my example, the rating group is configured for integrated billing, so the billing document is created as part of the configured rating process.

Consequently, there is no need to execute a separate billable-item billing run using transaction FKKBIXBIT_MON for this particular scenario.

This behavior depends on the integrated-billing configuration and should not be assumed for every CI implementation:

Transaction: FICAIMG >> Contract Accounts Receivable and Payable >> Convergent Invoicing >> Rating >> Define Rating Groups

The resulting billing document contains the calculated availability bonus. It also carries the quantity and unit of measurement entered in the consumption item, provided the relevant billing-quantity interface component is selected in the billable item class.

Billing document 347 including amount, quantity, and unit of measurement.

Billable Item Class ZV2G with interface component “Billing quantity”.

This completes the CI calculation of the availability bonus. The next step is to integrate the resulting billing document into the IS-U invoicing process.

5. Executing the invoicing run in IS-U

We now have two billing documents:

  • An IS-U billing document containing the charging and discharging quantities measured in kWh.
  • A CI billing document containing the availability bonus calculated from the connection duration.

The objective is to process both documents through IS-U invoicing so that the resulting customer invoice includes both components.

To ensure that both billing documents can be invoiced together, you need to customize the invoicing process in which you can specify the source document categories in the selection control.

Once your invoicing process is defined in the customizing, you also need to specify to which creation reason in IS-U it applies. For our scenario, we want our CI billing document to be invoiced on the same print document together with an IS-U billing document with source document type “01”:

EAINV_MON – Source document type.

When you invoice the contract account via transaction EAINV_MON, you will be asked to specify the invoicing process along with its compatible creation reason. After executing, the system will at one point call function ISU_INV_SELECT_DOCUMENTS which verifies whether the selected invoicing process is compatible with the creation reason of the IS-U billing document:

Function Module ISU_INV_SELECT_DOCUMENTS with CALL FUNCTION ‘ISU_DB_TE2602_SELECT’ on line 82.

As illustrated by the image above, the assignment between the creation reason and the invoicing process is stored in table TE2602:

Table TE2602: Assignment of invoicing procedure to creation reason.

If the required assignment is missing, the CI billing document may not be selected for joint invoicing through the intended IS-U invoicing process.

The relevant customizing activity is:

SAP Customizing Implementation Guide >> SAP Utilities >> Invoicing >> Integration with Convergent Invoicing >> Invoicing of Source Documents from Convergent Invoicing >> Assign Invoicing Process to Reasons for Creation

Once the required configuration is in place, the joint invoicing run can be executed. In my example, both transactions EAINV_MON and EA19 can be used to produce the joint invoicing result:

Joint invoicing of billing documents 347 (CI) and 100000005601 (IS-U) through EAINV_MON.

Joint invoicing of both billing documents 347 (CI) and 100000005601 (IS-U) through EA19.

Although both transactions produce the same result, I prefer EAINV_MON because it displays additional information such as target process. 

After executing the invoicing run and selecting the relevant source documents, the system successfully creates IS-U print document 2000000229:

Application log – print document 2000000229 successfully created.

By navigating to the Source Documents tab of the print document, we can identify the billing documents included in the invoicing process. In this example, the print document references the IS-U billing document 100000005601 (ERCH) and the CI billing document 347 (INVBI):

IS-U Print Document 2000000229 with source documents 100000005601 (ERCH) and 347 (INVBI).

This confirms that the two billing results have been brought together in a common IS-U invoicing process.

6. Final results: IS-U print document, Invoicing document and FI-CA posting documents

After successful joint invoicing, we can examine the resulting documents to understand how the IS-U and CI components are represented in the system.

6.1 IS-U Print Document

The resulting IS-U print document is 2000000229.

Its document overview shows the posting-relevant items originating from the IS-U billing process and the availability bonus calculated through CI.

IS-U Print document 2000000229 - Document Overview.

As shown in the image above, I did not apply any tax amounts for the availability bonus just as I did in the previous part of this series (V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 3) : From Measured Quantities to Billing and Invoicing). For the invoicing document that will be created through CI, you can configure this in posting area 2610 by linking the required tax determination to your company code, main and sub-transactions and the targeted G/L account for postings to be made.

Account assignments on chart of accounts 2500 in posting area 2610.

6.2. CI Invoicing Document

The IS-U print document also provides a link to the associated CI invoicing document.

In this example, the CI invoicing document number is 7000000116. It can be identified through the relevant reference field in table ERDK in the demonstrated system.

Invoicing document 7000000116 in table field ERDK- INVDOCNO.

To examine the document in more detail, we can use transaction FKKINVDOC_DISP.

The CI invoicing document contains the relevant invoicing information for the availability bonus, including the items processed through CI and the applicable integration information.

Invoicing document 7000000116 in FKKINVDOC_DISP.

This provides a useful way to trace the availability bonus from its original consumption item through rating and billing to the final invoicing result.

6.3. FI-CA Posting Documents

Finally, we can examine the FI-CA postings created as part of the invoicing process.

In this example, the system creates two FI-CA posting documents: one for the items originating from IS-U and another for the availability bonus originating from CI.

The documents are 5000000702 and 5000000703, and both refer to the common IS-U print document 2000000229:

Two documents posted in FI-CA:  5000000702 and 5000000703.

Table DFKKOP: posting documents 5000000702 and 5000000703 representing the total amount of IS-U print document 2000000229.

This distinction is important. Although the customer-facing result is a common IS-U print document, the underlying financial processing can retain separate FI-CA documents for the IS-U and CI components.

The example therefore illustrates how the availability bonus can be calculated independently in CI and integrated into the IS-U invoicing process without requiring both components to originate from the same billing engine.

 

Conclusion

With this final chapter, we have explored an alternative approach to integrating a V2G availability bonus into the SAP IS-U Meter-to-Cash process by leveraging Convergent Invoicing.

By retaining the conventional IS-U metering and billing setup for charging and discharging quantities in kWh, we can calculate the availability bonus separately in CI based on the vehicle's connection time. The resulting CI billing document can then be integrated into the IS-U invoicing process, allowing both billing results to be included in a common IS-U print document.

We have also followed the process beyond billing and invoicing, examining the resulting CI invoicing document and the separate FI-CA postings generated for the IS-U and CI components.

This approach demonstrates one possible way to combine the capabilities of SAP IS-U and Convergent Invoicing while avoiding additional IS-U configuration to register the availability duration in minutes.

I hope this four-part V2G series has provided useful insights into the different possibilities for implementing Vehicle-to-Grid scenarios in SAP Utilities.

Thank you for following the series! I would be very interested to hear your thoughts:

Would you implement the availability bonus directly in IS-U, or would you consider Convergent Invoicing for this purpose?

Feel free to share your experiences and alternative approaches in the comments.

SAP Service Cloud Version 2 is SAP's modern customer service solution that helps organizations manage customer interactions, cases, service processes, knowledge management, omnichannel communications, and agent productivity from a unified platform. It provides a modern agent desktop, advanced case management capabilities, workflow automation, AI-driven recommendations, and seamless integration with the broader SAP ecosystem.

Simplify and personalize service requests
Improve issue resolution speed
Increase service agent productivity
Deliver omnichannel customer support
Automate service operations
Leverage AI-driven insights and recommendations
Why SAP Introduced Version 2?

SAP Service Cloud V2 is not just an upgrade. It is a complete modernization of the service platform designed around modern cloud principles and intelligent automation.The new platform focuses on:

  • Enhanced user experience
  • Improved scalability
  • Faster innovation cycles
  • Embedded AI capabilities
  • Flexible integrations
  • Cloud-native architecture

SAP Service Cloud V2 addresses these challenges with a combination of automation, AI, omnichannel service, and intelligent case management.

  • Faster issue resolution

  • Improved customer satisfaction

  • Cases
  • Activities
  • Knowledge articles
  • Related business objects into a single interface.

Why It Matters?

Agents spend less time searching for information and more time solving customer issues.

Modern customers communicate through multiple channels.Service Cloud V2 supports interaction management across:

  • Email
  • Chat
  • Phone
  • Other integrated communication channels

The platform ensures service agents have visibility into customer interactions regardless of the channel used.

Artificial Intelligence is deeply embedded within SAP's customer experience strategy.

SAP Service Cloud uses AI to:

  • Improve agent productivity
  • Automate routine tasks
  • Support intelligent service processes

SAP positions AI as a key capability for improving efficiency and customer satisfaction.

Agents can:

  • Share service-related content
  • Collaborate with colleagues
  • Discuss service cases
  • Stay informed through real-time updates without leaving their service processes.

Business Benefit:

Improved collaboration and faster decision making.

Service organizations frequently need visibility into installed products and assets.

SAP Service Cloud V2 supports:

  • Registered products
  • Warranty information
  • Customer-linked assets

entry.title: Da revisão do forecast à decisão: como coordenar pessoas, versões e tarefas no SAC
entry.content:
Considere um cenário hipotético de fechamento mensal com três unidades. Não há aqui uma implantação real nem resultados medidos. A situação serve para discutir uma distinção prática: trabalhar os números, revisar seu conteúdo e decidir sobre a publicação são responsabilidades que precisam ser explicitadas.

No SAP Analytics Cloud (SAC), recursos de planejamento e colaboração podem apoiar essas atividades. O método proposto é conectá-los sem tratar comentário, tarefa concluída e versão publicada como se fossem a mesma coisa.

1. Defina a revisão antes de distribuir trabalho

Forecast é a previsão usada para acompanhar o planejamento. A revisão precisa começar com uma definição compartilhada:

Qual previsão está em discussão, para qual período, em quais unidades e para apoiar qual decisão?

A recomendação é registrar também qual versão está sendo trabalhada. Sem essa referência, pedir apenas que cada responsável “atualize seus números” não explicita a relação entre a contribuição individual e o cenário em análise.

No exemplo hipotético, a equipe central poderia combinar o recorte da revisão e a versão de trabalho antes de distribuir tarefas. Isso é uma escolha de processo apoiada pela gestão de versões, não uma promessa de que a ferramenta definirá o processo pela organização.

2. Versão privada é espaço de trabalho, não publicação

A gestão de versões permite trabalhar nos próprios dados antes de publicar, explorar cenários e fazer análise de desvios. Também oferece recursos para desfazer e refazer mudanças, consultar histórico e retornar uma versão privada a um estado anterior.

Na revisão proposta, cada responsável poderia usar uma versão privada para testar suas mudanças. O ponto não é produzir cenários sem critério. É preservar a distinção entre uma hipótese em elaboração e os dados que se pretende publicar.

Se a discussão apontar outra direção, o histórico e a possibilidade de retornar a um estado anterior fazem parte desse trabalho. Não é necessário apresentar cada tentativa como a previsão já decidida.

A pergunta de controle, portanto, não deve ser somente “você terminou?”. Deve incluir:

“Qual versão foi revisada e o que ainda precisa ser decidido antes da publicação?”

A resposta precisa estar no processo, não ser presumida a partir de uma tela.

3. Confira o recorte e o que a validação realmente garante

Uma story é o ambiente de relatório e análise do SAC, com tabelas, gráficos e elementos interativos. Ela pode apoiar a conversa sobre os números. Mas a navegação na análise também precisa de contexto.

Bookmarks, por exemplo, guardam filtros e prompts, isto é, parâmetros de seleção. Não são substitutos da versão de dados de planejamento. Para a revisão, recomendo identificar tanto o cenário em trabalho quanto o recorte exibido, sem confundir uma visão salva com uma publicação.

Outra camada são as regras de validação. Elas definem combinações permitidas entre membros de dimensões e impedem operações de planejamento fora dessas combinações.

É uma verificação específica: passar por uma combinação permitida não deve ser apresentado como prova de que uma premissa de negócio foi aprovada.

Há ainda os bloqueios de dados. Eles permitem proteger recortes, delegar responsáveis e restringir a edição aos donos. Mudanças nos bloqueios podem ser programadas no calendário.

Antes de incorporar isso ao fechamento, é preciso verificar a configuração aplicável, em vez de pressupor que todo recorte já está protegido.

4. Dê responsáveis e revisores ao trabalho

O calendário do SAC permite criar tarefas, atribuir pessoas à execução e designar outras para revisar. Processos podem reunir várias tarefas. Também há acompanhamento de status, prazos e lembretes.

No cenário hipotético, essas capacidades podem organizar as contribuições das três unidades e suas revisões.

Para cada tarefa, a recomendação é deixar claro:

  • Executor: quem realiza a atividade.

  • Revisor: quem verifica o trabalho realizado.

  • Prazo: quando a atividade deve ser concluída.

Isso não significa que criar uma tarefa estabeleça automaticamente o vínculo com uma versão privada ou publique seus dados.

O calendário organiza trabalho e acompanhamento; a decisão sobre o conteúdo e sua publicação precisa continuar explícita.

Ao consultar o andamento, a equipe central deve perguntar o que aquele status representa no processo definido.

“Concluído” pode descrever o trabalho atribuído, mas não deve ser usado, por inferência, como declaração de que toda a previsão foi aprovada e publicada.

5. Use o feedback no contexto adequado

Comentários podem ser feitos em uma página da story, em um ponto de dado ou em um widget, que é um elemento da análise. Também é possível mencionar pessoas.

Discussões permitem conversar com usuários e equipes, incluir anexos e relacionar outras stories.

Na revisão hipotética, um revisor poderia registrar uma pergunta sobre a premissa de uma previsão no ponto relevante da análise. A discussão com a equipe poderia reunir a conversa necessária para esclarecer a dúvida.

Não estamos atribuindo valor financeiro nem desfecho a esse exemplo.

O critério é simples:

  • Comentários: localizar dúvidas e observações no contexto da análise.

  • Discussões: facilitar a troca de informações entre pessoas e equipes.

Esses recursos são meios de feedback e colaboração. Não devem ser tratados como aprovação formal só porque alguém respondeu ou foi mencionado.

6. Um fluxo ilustrativo, sem automatismos presumidos

Para a Controladoria do exemplo, o método poderia seguir esta ordem:

 

Etapa 1. Preparar a revisão

Definir previsão, período, unidades e versão de trabalho.

 

Etapa 2. Atribuir contribuições

Indicar executores, revisores e prazos nas tarefas.

Etapa 3. Trabalhar os cenários

Testar mudanças em versões privadas e consultar o histórico quando necessário.

Etapa 4. Conferir o conteúdo

Revisar o recorte na story, registrar dúvidas e verificar regras de validação e bloqueios aplicáveis.

Etapa 5. Decidir sobre a publicação

Identificar quem pode realizá-la e em quais condições.

Etapa 6. Acompanhar o encerramento

Consultar status e pendências sem equiparar conclusão de tarefa a publicação dos dados.

É uma proposta de organização baseada em capacidades descritas, não uma sequência automaticamente executada pelo SAC.

Não se promete que concluir uma etapa valide o mérito econômico da previsão ou dispare a próxima ação.

Também há um limite de acesso: na base consultada, licença BI permite entrada básica em modelos de planejamento e criação de versões privadas; publicação de versões e uso de ferramentas de planejamento exigem licença de planejamento.

Licenças e permissões precisam ser verificadas antes de distribuir responsabilidades.

 

Conclusão

A revisão fica mais bem definida quando versão de trabalho, verificação do dado e responsabilidade das pessoas deixam de ser uma única ideia chamada “finalizar o forecast”.

No seu processo, quem assume explicitamente a responsabilidade pela validação antes de a versão ser publicada?

entry.title: Reading classic dynpro flow logic remotely over ADT (HTTP): is there an endpoint, or only RFC?
entry.content:
Hi all,

This morning I was answering a question about the partner tab in VA01 (function group V09C, screen 1000), and I wanted to read the flow logic of that screen to see which modules run inside LOOP WITH CONTROL. I read most standard code through ADT, and for classes, function modules and includes everything is there. For classic screens I got stuck.

What I checked, on S/4HANA 2023 (SAP_BASIS 758) and S/4HANA 2025 (816):

  • The ADT discovery document (/sap/bc/adt/discovery) has no collection for classic screens in either release. The only "screen" in it is the value help for logical database selection screens.
  • The where-used list does know the screen: a where-used on PBO module IS_ENHANCEMENT_01 returns screen 1000 as object type FUGR/PS, with a /sap/bc/adt/vit/wb/... URI. I haven't found a source endpoint behind it.
  • Over RFC there is a way: SVRS_GET_VERSION_DYNP_40 is RFC-enabled and has a D022S_TAB table parameter, which is the flow logic. IMPORT_DYNPRO is RFC-enabled too, but it returns only the header (D020S) and the fields (D021S). RPY_DYNPRO_READ has everything, but it is not RFC-enabled.

So my question: is there an ADT (HTTP) endpoint that returns the flow logic of a classic screen, read-only, that I'm missing? Or is the honest answer "SAP GUI or RFC"?

And if you work with ADT in VS Code or in Eclipse without SAP GUI, how do you look at PBO/PAI today?

In the V09C case I got around it from the other side: SAP's own IS-Oil enhancement implementation OIG_SAPLV09C_01 works on the current table control line, so that module has to run inside the loop. But I would like to see it, not deduce it.

entry.title: Antes do dashboard: como escolher conexão, dataset e modelo no SAP Analytics Cloud
entry.content:
Esse é um cenário hipotético de Controladoria, não um relato de implantação. Ele ajuda a separar decisões que parecem uma só quando o pedido chega como “precisamos de um dashboard”. No SAP Analytics Cloud, ou SAC, escolher a base analítica envolve conexão, estrutura dos dados e finalidade de uso. A visualização vem depois dessas escolhas.

Comece pelo que precisa ser entendido

No exemplo, “despesas por centro de custo” ainda deixa espaço para esclarecer o recorte. A equipe quer investigar uma dúvida pontual ou estabelecer uma análise governada? Precisa apenas consultar valores ou também trabalhar com números de planejamento?

Essas perguntas têm correspondência na estrutura analítica. Dimensões são categorias que dão perspectiva aos números, como centro de custo e data. Medidas são os valores numéricos analisados. Um modelo reúne dimensões e medidas para representar um conjunto específico de dados.

Por isso, antes de escolher a apresentação, vale escrever a pergunta com seu contexto: qual valor será observado, por quais categorias e para qual finalidade? No cenário hipotético, essa descrição não precisa antecipar a resposta. Precisa deixar claro o que a equipe pretende analisar.

Conexão é uma decisão com restrições

A conexão permite a comunicação entre o SAC e uma fonte de dados, que pode estar na nuvem ou em ambiente local. Ela é específica para a fonte: trabalhar com diferentes origens exige considerar suas respectivas conexões.

Há dois tipos descritos para esse acesso: live e importação. A escolha não deve começar pela preferência por um nome. Os critérios incluem necessidades funcionais, restrições de privacidade e volume de dados. Também é necessário verificar requisitos técnicos e suporte para a versão e o tipo de conexão utilizados.

Para a Controladoria do exemplo, a recomendação é transformar esses critérios em perguntas à equipe responsável pela fonte. O acesso pretendido é suportado? As exigências de privacidade estão contempladas? Há restrições de volume ou funcionalidades que precisam ser consideradas?

Sem essas respostas, não cabe prometer que qualquer origem atenderá a qualquer desenho. Tampouco cabe declarar live ou importação como solução superior em todos os casos. A decisão precisa corresponder ao ambiente efetivo da organização.

Dataset ou modelo: escolha pela finalidade

Um dataset é uma coleção simples de dados, normalmente organizada em tabela, que pode servir de base para uma story. Story é o nome usado no SAC para esse objeto de análise. Dataset e modelo podem sustentá-lo, mas atendem a necessidades diferentes.

Datasets se destinam a análises simples e ad hoc: explorações pontuais, sem a mesma proposta de governança dos modelos. Modelos são indicados quando a análise exige uma base mais governada ou envolve planejamento. Não se trata de escolher o objeto “mais sofisticado”, e sim aquele coerente com o uso.

No cenário hipotético, uma investigação pontual de despesas pode ser discutida como exploração. Se o objetivo for uma análise governada, a conversa passa a ser sobre modelo. A recorrência do pedido deve motivar essa discussão, mas não substitui a definição do nível de governança necessário.

Há ainda uma separação importante: modelos analíticos são de leitura; modelos de planejamento permitem leitura e escrita. Estes requerem as dimensões Data e Versão, e a escrita depende de permissões de planejamento. Datasets não suportam casos de planejamento.

Logo, se o pedido evoluir de “entender despesas” para “trabalhar uma previsão”, não convém tratar essa mudança apenas como inclusão de uma coluna no painel. A finalidade precisa ser reavaliada à luz do modelo adequado e das permissões envolvidas.

Um exemplo concreto, com fronteiras claras

Um caso documentado de modelo live utiliza SAP HANA em ambiente local. O procedimento seleciona uma visão de cálculo, define a data do pedido como dimensão temporal e visualiza os dados no Data Analyzer.

O exemplo mostra uma combinação específica entre origem, conexão, estrutura e análise. Não demonstra que a fonte de despesas do cenário hipotético está disponível, nem autoriza generalizar o mesmo caminho para todas as origens.

Na criação do modelo live, o tipo de sistema, a conexão e a fonte precisam corresponder à organização. Esse é o ponto aproveitável para a decisão de negócio: pedir a validação da combinação real, em vez de transformar um exemplo técnico em promessa de compatibilidade.

Explore o recorte antes de fechar o desenho

O Data Analyzer é uma aplicação pronta para análise ad hoc. Ele permite trabalhar com visualização em tabela ou gráfico, aplicar filtros e adicionar ou remover dimensões e medidas. Também permite salvar o estado de detalhamento e a análise como um insight.

Na aplicação hipotética, depois de confirmar uma fonte suportada, a equipe poderia testar o recorte de despesas por centro de custo e observar os detalhes necessários. O objetivo dessa etapa seria esclarecer a análise desejada, não afirmar que um resultado financeiro já foi obtido.

Ao salvar o insight, é possível informar nome e descrição. Isso oferece uma forma de guardar o recorte explorado para a discussão sobre o que se deseja visualizar.

Há uma fronteira que merece ficar explícita: medidas calculadas criadas nessa análise existem apenas no insight e não são transferidas para a fonte de dados. Se a equipe usar um cálculo exploratório, precisa tratá-lo como tal, sem apresentá-lo como alteração na origem.

Um checklist antes de solicitar a story

Para conduzir a conversa, proponho cinco verificações:

  • Escrever a pergunta e identificar medidas e dimensões relevantes.

  • Confirmar fonte, suporte da conexão, privacidade, volume e requisitos técnicos.

  • Distinguir exploração pontual de análise governada.

  • Verificar se haverá planejamento e, nesse caso, qual modelo e quais permissões são necessários.

  • Explorar um recorte no Data Analyzer, quando aplicável, e registrar o insight sem confundir cálculo local com mudança na fonte.

Esse roteiro organiza critérios; não dispensa a validação de suporte e configuração no ambiente utilizado. O dashboard é uma forma de apresentar a análise, não uma resposta automática às decisões sobre sua base.

Antes de discutir qual gráfico usar, qual critério pesa mais na sua escolha: a restrição da fonte, a governança da análise ou a necessidade de planejamento?

entry.title: Introducing new 'Monitor Alerts' application in SAP Asset Performance Management
entry.content:
Alex starts every shift the same way. Open Monitor Alerts, scan the queue, figure out what needs attention. On a quiet day that takes ten minutes. On a bad day, it takes all morning - not because the alerts are complex, but because getting the full picture means bouncing between applications, chasing down who looked at something last, and eventually giving up and just starting from scratch.

Alert management sounds simple in theory. An indicator breaches a threshold, an alert is raised, someone investigates, and maintenance action follows. In practice, it is rarely that clean.

The alert exists, but who owns it? What happened before it was raised? Has anyone already acted on it? Where is the full picture of this asset's health? The old Monitor Alerts application gave you the alert. Getting answers to those questions meant going elsewhere.

In release 2610, SAP Asset Performance Management introduces a significantly improved Monitor Alerts experience - rebuilt on the SAP Cloud Application Programming (CAP) framework. That is not just a technical detail. CAP is what makes the application extensible, structured, and ready to grow with your process. And it is what enables the new capabilities that ship alongside it.

A complete workflow, in one place

Start with context

Alex glances at the Monitor Alerts tile on his Fiori launchpad to see how many brand new alerts are waiting.  Today there are 19 new alerts waiting.

SAP APM Fiori launchpad showing the new Monitor Alerts tile with 19 alerts highlighted in the Asset Health Monitoring section, alongside the legacy application.

A VIBRATION_SURGE alert has landed in Alex's queue. A centrifugal pump has a sudden spike in vibration, and this is not the first time. Before deciding anything, Alex needs to know whether this is a recurring pattern or an isolated event - and what the pump's broader health looks like right now.

The new Monitor Alerts application answers that without making you leave it. The Indicator Monitoring tab now includes an Additional Information section with a direct link to the Explore Technical Objects application. One click opens all associated alerts and the full indicator chart for that technical object, in a new tab. You stay in context. You get the data you need to make a call.

Monitor Alerts detail view for a Vibration Surge alert, showing the Indicator Monitoring tab with the Additional Information section — selecting the Centrifugal Pump 1 CM link opens the Explore Technical Objects application.

For more information, see Viewing Alerts

Put someone in charge

Alex investigates and it is clear this one needs a closer look - but Alex is heading into a planning meeting in twenty minutes. Someone else needs to pick it up.

The new Assigned To field lets you designate a processor for each alert directly in Monitor Alerts. Everyone on the team can see who is handling what, which means less duplication and fewer things falling through the gaps.

Vibration Surge alert in edit mode, showing the Administrative Information section with the Assigned To field highlighted, where you can enter the responsible processor.

The alert does not sit in a shared queue waiting for someone to claim it. It has an owner.

For more information, see Assigning a Processor to an Alert.

Know exactly what happened

Later that day, a colleague asks about the same pump unit. Alex pulls up the alert and everything is there - who looked at it, when the status changed, what follow-up was linked.

Every change to an alert is now recorded in a dedicated Change Log tab. Status updates, reassignments, linked follow-up actions - all of it is captured automatically. If you need to understand what happened to an alert and when, the answer is right there.

Vibration Surge alert Change Log tab showing two entries - a notification created with number 12851897 and a status update from New to In Process - recording who made each change and when

For more information, see Alert Change Log.

Turn insights into action without switching systems

The pattern is confirmed. This pump needs a maintenance notification. Alex used to have to open S/4HANA separately, find the right equipment record, and create the notification from scratch.

Now you can create a Maintenance Notification in SAP S/4HANA directly from Monitor Alerts. And when you do, you can optionally set a Detection Method - a field that captures how the failure was discovered. Was it flagged during a planned inspection? Picked up by condition monitoring? That information feeds back into failure analysis and helps teams improve how they detect and respond over time.

For more information, see Create Notification.

He can also now navigate directly from Monitor Alerts to the corresponding S/4HANA Maintenance Notification. No switching between systems manually, and no searching for the right record.

Built to be extended

Alex works in a large industrial operation with workflows and terminology that do not map perfectly to any out-of-the-box application. That used to mean workarounds.

Because Monitor Alerts is built on CAP, it supports SaaS extensibility. If your organization needs to adapt the application to specific workflows, add custom fields, or integrate with other services, the Cloud Application Programming framework gives you the foundation to do that in a structured, upgrade-safe way.

For more information, see Extending Multi-Service Applications.

To sum up

By the time Alex closes out for the day, the queue looks different. Alerts have owners. The change log shows exactly what happened and when. A maintenance notification is already in S/4HANA. And nothing fell through the cracks.

Better navigation. Clear ownership. Full traceability. Direct integration with SAP S/4HANA. And a foundation built for the future.

Check out the links given above to the SAP Help Portal.

Co-author: Kate Dowle

entry.title: From Nonconformances to Action: Connecting n8n, AI, and SAP Digital Manufacturing
entry.content:
Introduction

After my first hands-on experiment with n8n and SAP Digital Manufacturing, where I retrieved manufacturing alerts and used an AI Agent to summarize and prioritize them, I decided to take the next step.

This time, I wanted to explore a manufacturing quality scenario: how can we use AI to analyze open nonconformances, provide actionable recommendations to production supervisors, and automatically raise alerts for critical issues directly in SAP Digital Manufacturing?

The idea is simple. Manufacturing systems already capture valuable information about production issues, but identifying the right priorities and deciding what to do next can require time and manual effort.

By combining SAP Digital Manufacturing, n8n, and a Large Language Model (LLM), we can build a workflow that transforms nonconformance data into actionable insights and connects critical findings back to the manufacturing system.

Let's explore how it works!

The use case

In this scenario, we want to help a production supervisor understand the current nonconformance situation and react quickly when critical quality issues arise.

The workflow has two parallel paths:

  • AI-powered analysis: Retrieve open nonconformances, analyze them using an LLM, generate insights and recommendations, and deliver a summary to the supervisor by email and Microsoft Teams.

  • Critical issue handling: Identify critical nonconformances and automatically create alerts in SAP Digital Manufacturing so the supervisor can follow up directly in the manufacturing system.

This combination is what makes the example interesting. We are not just generating a report or sending a notification. We are connecting manufacturing data, AI-generated insights, and operational actions in one workflow.

The technology stack

For this experiment, I used three main components.

SAP Digital Manufacturing

SAP Digital Manufacturing provides the manufacturing context and operational data. In this scenario, it is the source of the nonconformance records and the destination for alerts created for critical issues.

n8n

n8n orchestrates the workflow. It connects the different services, retrieves data through HTTP requests, applies filters, invokes the LLM, and coordinates the delivery of insights and the creation of alerts.

One of the interesting aspects of n8n is how quickly we can combine APIs, data transformations, AI capabilities, and business applications using a visual workflow.

Large Language Model (LLM)

The LLM reviews the open nonconformance data and generates a structured summary with relevant observations, recommendations, and suggested next steps.

For this implementation, the workflow uses the Basic LLM Chain node connected to an SAP AI Core model.

The LLM does not replace the manufacturing system or its business rules. Instead, it helps interpret the available information and turn it into something more useful for the person responsible for production.

Step 1: Retrieve nonconformances from SAP Digital Manufacturing

The workflow starts with a manual execution trigger in n8n, which is useful during development and testing.

In real-life manufacturing scenarios, this process can be fully automated using a Schedule Trigger to periodically check for new or updated nonconformances, or an event-driven approach that starts the workflow when a relevant event occurs in SAP Digital Manufacturing, provided the required integration mechanisms are available.

For example, the workflow could run every 15 minutes to analyze open nonconformances and notify production supervisors, while critical issues could trigger immediate alerts. With appropriate safeguards to prevent duplicate processing and handle API failures, this approach can become part of a continuous monitoring process, helping teams identify issues and take action faster.

Once it starts, an HTTP Request node retrieves nonconformance records from SAP Digital Manufacturing through an API call.

The returned data is then passed to a Split Out node, which separates the collection into individual items. This makes it easier to process each nonconformance independently in the following steps.

Next, a Filter node selects the records whose status is OPEN.

Step 2: Use AI to generate insights and recommendations

Once the open nonconformances have been identified, the workflow passes them to a Basic LLM Chain connected to SAP AI Core.

The objective is to go beyond listing records.

Instead of asking the supervisor to review every nonconformance individually, we can ask the LLM to analyze the available information and prepare a concise, actionable summary.

For example, the analysis can focus on:

  • The most relevant open nonconformances.

  • Recurring issues or patterns visible in the supplied data.

  • Potential production or quality risks.

  • Recommended investigation or follow-up steps.

  • Which issues deserve the supervisor's attention first.

The quality of the results depends on the information available in the source records and the instructions provided to the model.

For example, if the nonconformance records contain a description, material, work center, severity, timestamps, and other relevant attributes, these fields can provide useful context for the analysis.

However, the LLM should not be expected to discover information that is not present in the data. Recommendations should be presented as suggestions based on the available evidence, not as confirmed root causes.

Designing the LLM instructions

A useful prompt should clearly define the role, the task, and the expected output.

For example:

Role: You are a manufacturing quality analyst supporting a production supervisor.

Task: Review the supplied open nonconformances and prepare an actionable summary.

Instructions:

  1. Identify the most relevant issues requiring attention.

  2. Group similar issues when the available data supports doing so.

  3. Explain why each highlighted issue deserves attention.

  4. Suggest practical investigation and follow-up steps.

  5. Distinguish facts found in the records from hypotheses or recommendations.

  6. Do not invent missing information or claim that a root cause has been confirmed without evidence.

  7. Use clear, concise language suitable for a production supervisor.

Expected output: A short executive summary followed by prioritized issues, supporting observations, and recommended next steps.

This is only an illustrative prompt. The actual instructions should be adapted to the available fields, the manufacturing process, and the organization's quality procedures.

The objective is to make the output useful for decision-making rather than simply producing a long text summary.

Step 3: Send the insights by email and Microsoft Teams

After the AI analysis, the workflow follows the communication path.

A Summarize node prepares the output, which is then sent through two channels:

  • Email: The supervisor receives a summary of the open nonconformances, relevant insights, recommendations, and suggested actions.

  • Microsoft Teams: A chat message delivers the information through another channel already used for collaboration.

Using both channels can make the information easier to access, depending on how the production team works.

Email

Microsoft Teams

The content should be concise enough to review quickly, while providing sufficient detail for the supervisor to decide which issues require investigation.

A useful message could contain:

  • A brief overview of the current situation.

  • The most relevant nonconformances.

  • Why each issue matters.

  • Recommended next steps.

  • References or identifiers that allow the supervisor to locate the original records.

The goal is not to overwhelm the production team with another notification. It is to provide the right context to support faster and better-informed decisions.

Step 4: Identify critical nonconformances and create alerts in SAP Digital Manufacturing

Now comes the second path in the workflow.

In parallel with the AI analysis, the workflow applies another Filter node to identify nonconformances classified as CRITICAL.

The records that pass this filter are sent to an HTTP Request node, which creates alerts directly in SAP Digital Manufacturing.

This is an important distinction.

The AI analysis supports the supervisor by interpreting the available information and suggesting actions. The criticality filter, on the other hand, applies an explicit condition to determine which records should trigger the alert-creation process.

In this implementation, the criticality filter is based on the data and criteria configured in the workflow. It is not the LLM deciding which records qualify as critical.

This approach allows the workflow to combine flexible AI-generated recommendations with predictable, rule-based handling of critical issues.

Why create alerts in SAP Digital Manufacturing?

Sending an email or a Teams message informs the supervisor, but creating an alert in the manufacturing system connects the issue to the operational environment where production activities are managed.

This provides a more direct path from detecting a critical nonconformance to initiating follow-up.

The alert can help draw attention to the issue within SAP Digital Manufacturing, subject to the alert configuration and the way the production team manages alerts.

For a production-ready implementation, it is important to define the alert content carefully, including the nonconformance identifier, a meaningful description, and any relevant context that helps the supervisor investigate.

The API request must also follow the alert-creation requirements of the target SAP Digital Manufacturing environment.

The complete workflow

See the complete n8n workflow below:

In the actual n8n implementation, the criticality filter branches from the output of the Basic LLM Chain node, as shown in the workflow screenshot. If the objective is to make critical alert creation independent of LLM execution and availability, the branch can be connected earlier, directly after the relevant filtering or data-preparation step.

That is an important architectural consideration: critical operational notifications should not depend unnecessarily on the successful completion of an AI analysis.

From insights to action: closing the loop

What makes this scenario more interesting than a conventional reporting workflow is the connection between analysis, communication, and operational follow-up.

Consider the following sequence:

  1. SAP Digital Manufacturing provides the nonconformance data.

  2. n8n filters the records to identify open issues.

  3. An LLM analyzes the available information and proposes recommendations.

  4. The supervisor receives the insights through email and Microsoft Teams.

  5. Critical nonconformances trigger alerts in SAP Digital Manufacturing.

  6. The supervisor can investigate the issues and initiate the appropriate follow-up.

This creates the foundation for an insight-to-action loop.

The workflow does not automatically resolve a nonconformance, confirm a root cause, or guarantee that the recommended actions are completed. Those activities remain dependent on the supervisor, the manufacturing process, and the systems used to manage corrective actions.

However, the workflow can reduce the effort required to collect information, highlight relevant issues, and initiate follow-up.

That is already a meaningful opportunity for improvement.

Conclusion

This second n8n experiment builds on my first workflow with SAP Digital Manufacturing and takes the idea a step further.

Instead of simply retrieving manufacturing data and generating a summary, we are combining:

  • Operational data from SAP Digital Manufacturing.

  • AI-powered analysis using an LLM.

  • Actionable insights delivered through email and Microsoft Teams.

  • Rule-based identification of critical nonconformances.

  • Automated alert creation directly in SAP Digital Manufacturing.

The most interesting part is the combination of AI and traditional workflow automation. The LLM helps interpret information and suggest next steps, while explicit filters and API calls connect the results to operational processes.

We do not need to automate everything at once to start creating value. Even a focused use case can help us learn, validate ideas, and identify opportunities for improvement.

I'm excited to keep exploring how tools like n8n, combined with SAP Digital Manufacturing and AI services, can help transform manufacturing data into timely, actionable insights.

What manufacturing scenario would you automate first?

Do you want to see more content like this? Please live a Like!

Best,

Manoel Costa

@bigflatfoot thanks for the context in your comment, now the case is clear. I'm answering here because the code doesn't fit in a comment.

Then it depends on one thing: should the ship-to be locked in every order of that type, or only when the order was created with reference?

In every order: no code. In the partner determination procedure of the order type (VOPA), flag Ship-to (SH) with "No change possible". I read SETUP_TC_FIELDS_1000 again for this: with the flag, the partner number closes as soon as it has a value, and a copied partner always has one. The functions without the flag stay open.

Only when created with reference: the same enhancement point IS_ENHANCEMENT_01_01, with one condition. The partner screen itself doesn't know about the reference, but the IS-Oil implementation in this same point shows how SAP solved it: it reads the caller's data with a dynamic ASSIGN of '(SAPMOIGS)T180'. For VA01 and VA02 the caller is SAPMV45A, where VBAK is a TABLES work area, and VBAK-VGBEL is the reference document. Something like this:

field-symbols <ls_vbak> type vbak.

assign ('(SAPMV45A)VBAK') to <ls_vbak>.
if <ls_vbak> is assigned and <ls_vbak>-vgbel is not initial.
  if gvs_tc_data-rec-parvw = 'WE'.   "ship-to: WE is the key, SH is the English display
    loop at screen.
      if screen-name = 'GVS_TC_DATA-REC-PARVW' or
         screen-name = 'GVS_TC_DATA-REC-PARTNER' or
         screen-name = 'GVS_TC_DATA-REC-PARTNER_EXT'.
        screen-input = 0.
        modify screen.
      endif.
    endloop.
  endif.
endif.

If your list of editable functions is shorter than the list of locked ones, I would turn the IF around and name the editable ones. In deliveries or billing SAPMV45A is not loaded, so the ASSIGN finds nothing and the code does nothing.

What I checked on S/4HANA 2023: the snippet passes the syntax check, and VBAK-VGBEL is really filled. 8 of the 261 standard orders in my system have it, and the 7 orders whose items came from a reference all have it at header level too.

What I didn't do: run VA01 with reference to see VBAK-VGBEL already filled at the moment the Partner tab is built. The saved orders have it, but I didn't watch it at runtime. Two more points. The ASSIGN to another program's data is not a released interface, so an upgrade can change it (SAP's own implementation lives with the same risk). And locking the fields doesn't stop someone from deleting the line and adding a new ship-to. If that matters, a check at save in USEREXIT_SAVE_DOCUMENT_PREPARE (MV45AFZZ, where XVBPA has the order partners) closes that door.
