entry.title: Using OAuth2 Client Credentials to access REST APIs in SAP Sales/Service Cloud Version 2
entry.content:
Introduction

While Communication System-based integration in SAP Sales/Service Cloud Version 2 (for instance with SAP S/4HANA) relies on Basic Authentication or X.509 client certificates for inbound connections, you can use OAuth 2.0 with the Client Credentials grant type for accessing the REST APIs in machine-to-machine scenarios without setting up a communication system. Only a technical user needs to be created.

In this blog, I'll show you how to set up OAuth2 Client Credentials and configure them in two sample clients.

 

Why OAuth2 Client Credentials?

A high-level comparison with the previously mentioned methods:

  • Basic Auth is easy to implement and to use. However, it sends the secret (the password) "unencrypted" to the API endpoint, usually with every call. As long as HTTPS is in use, the connection itself is encrypted at the transport layer. However, if an attacker manages to eavesdrop on the connection (e.g., man-in-the-middle attack), the secret is known and could thus be used for unauthorized access to the target system. For that reason, you should only use it for testing purposes in test environments.
  • X.509 Client Certificates offer strong mutual authentication where the secret (in this case the private key) is never transmitted to the recipient. Instead, cryptographic computations on data that changes with every session prove the identity of the server and the client. But this comes with significant operational overhead: certificate issuance, rotation, revocation, and trust store management across every consumer.
  • OAuth2 shifts the model: Credentials are exchanged once at a dedicated authorization server, and the resulting short-lived access token is what travels across APIs. That means the secret never reaches the resource server (compared to Basic Auth).
    Tokens carry embedded scope and expiry information, and are usually signed (depending on the validation method), which limits the impact if intercepted. Signing and validating tokens happens "behind the scenes" for the caller and keeps this complexity away from them.
    The Client Credentials flow is OAuth2 stripped down for machine-to-machine communication: No user context, no browser redirect. Just a system identity authenticating against an authorization server and calling the actual API at the resource server.

 

Setting Up OAuth2 Client Credentials for REST APIs in SAP Sales/Service Cloud Version 2

1. Create a Technical Role for the API user

If you don't already have a technical role with all required permissions, create a new one:
Go to User Menu --> System Settings --> (Users and Control) --> Roles --> switch the view from Business Roles to Technical Roles

Assign the services that the API user(s), who get this role assigned later, need. You can assign this role to multiple technical users.
Don't forget to Active the role.

 

2. Create Technical User and assign the Technical Role

Go to User Menu --> System Settings --> (Users and Control) --> Users --> switch the view from Business Users to Technical Users

Create a new technical user using the [+] button. (In contrast to business users, technical users can be created without an employee.)
You don't need to assign a password or upload a certificate for this user. The OAuth settings will be maintained on a different screen. Also, the entered user name will not be used outside of the system. It is just for your reference/to identify it.
Assign the technical role and save the technical user. 

 

3. Open the technical user and Generate Client Credentials

A dialog will be displayed that lets you copy the clientid and the clientsecret.
Please note that the clientsecret will only be displayed once! (see next step)

After initially generating the Client Credentials, you can only view the clientid. You can't view the clientsecret. If you forget the clientsecret, you can only generate a new clientsecret.

After these steps, you can configure clients to use OAuth 2 with the Client Credentials grant type to access SAP Sales and Service Cloud Version 2's REST APIs. Pay attention to additional properties that OAuth2 requires for handing over tokens, etc. I'll mention two examples for common clients in the next section.

 

Configuring Clients

Bruno API Client

In Bruno, you can set up OAuth 2.0  with the Client Credentials Grant Type on the Auth tab, either for a single request, or for a folder or collection, which allows you to inherit this Auth method to all requests in that folder or collection.

The following screenshot shows the most relevant elements of the Auth tab maintained for a single request that fetches the first 3 accounts from the system.
Maintain the following configuration attributes:

  • Access Token URL: https://<<SSCV2_HOST>>/oauth/token
  • Client ID: <<your client id>>
  • Client Secret: <<your client secret>>
  • Add Credentials to: Basic Auth Header

For the Token attributes, I could use the Bruno defaults: 

  • Token Source: Access Token
  • Token ID: credentials
  • Add token to: Headers
  • Header Prefix: Bearer

After you've maintained all the authentication details, you can click Get Access Token or directly send the request, which fetches the access token on demand.

 

SAP Integration Suite / Cloud Integration

The second example demonstrates how to call SAP Sales/Service Cloud v2's Accounts REST API (the same service as above in Bruno) from an integration flow (iFlow) in SAP Integration Suite/Cloud Integration using OAuth2 Client Credentials. This requires two steps:

  1. Create a Security Material
  2. Use the Security Material in an iFlow

1. Create the Security Material

In SAP Integration Suite, go to Monitor --> Integrations and APIs --> (Manage Security) --> Security Material
If you don't see the Create button on this screen, make sure the Runtime filter is set to All.
Choose Create --> OAuth2 Client Credentials and maintain the following attributes:

  • Name: <<credential name as later used in the iflow>>
  • Token Service URL: https://<<SSCV2_HOST>>/oauth/token
  • Grant Type: Send as Part of Body
  • Client ID: <<your client id>>
  • Client Secret: <<your client secret>>
  • Client Authentication: Send as Request Header
  • Content Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

The following screenshot shows the Manage Security Material screen. Make sure to adapt the default values of the highlighted fields.

 

After you have deployed the security material, you can use it in the iFlow.

 

2. Design the Integration Flow

The sample iFlow only consists of a single HTTP Request-Reply call to the Accounts REST API using the previously created security material. That means, the sample iFlow returns the first 3 accounts from SSCv2 as a JSON body to the iFlow caller.

The important properties can be found in the Connection tab:

  • Authentication must be set to OAuth2 Client Credentials
  • Credential Name must be set to the name of the previously created security material
    (in the sample screenshot below, the name is parameterized to allow users to configure it without editing the iFlow)

 

I hope this blog was helpful for getting started with OAuth2 Client Credentials in SAP Sales and Service Cloud Version 2.

entry.title: Joule A2A: MCP Gateway to S/4HANA with Principal Propagation
entry.content:
Joule A2A: MCP Gateway to S/4HANA with Principal Propagation

In a previous post we looked at connecting a custom A2A agent to S/4HANA Public Cloud with full principal propagation. But that approach comes with some drawbacks: hooking up individual APIs doesn't scale well, and it's hard to enforce governance. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for exposing tools and data to AI agents in a uniform way, and it's quickly becoming the common language between agents and enterprise systems. SAP's reference architecture for Agents and MCP positions Integration Suite as an MCP Gateway to safeguard traffic to enterprise systems — so this post extends the example to route a BTP-based agent through that gateway, still from customer-managed Joule.

Note: This post covers Customer-Managed Joule.

Scenario

We have an A2A-capable agent connected to Joule (customer-managed), with a destination that hands the Joule user's token to the agent on each A2A request. To reach S/4HANA Public Cloud, that agent now goes through the MCP Gateway: Integration Suite points its gateway at an S/4HANA OData service via a destination, the selected endpoints become MCP tools, and it all runs on Integration Cell. The user identity is propagated the whole way — from Joule, through the custom agent, through the MCP Gateway, into S/4HANA — so the backend call runs as the real user. And because the gateway sits on Integration Suite, we inherit the API Management controls we already know: additional authentication and authorization on top, plus IP filtering, rate limiting and quotas where we need them.

This matters because many customers have built their agents in an A2A manner, and their API policy often restricts them to endorsed architectures only.

Prerequisites

  • A working A2A agent and destination setup, as described in the principal propagation post
  • An S/4HANA Public Cloud system
  • Integration Suite, Premium Edition (only that Edition contains the MCP Gateway)

Step 1: Trust the Integration Suite subaccount in S/4

The very first step diverges from the previous post: the trust setup. Last time we configured S/4 to trust the destination certificate of the agent's subaccount. This time the piece that resolves the SAML Bearer assertion is the destination service of the subaccount where Integration Suite lives — and that is a different subaccount, with a different signing certificate (at least in my case). So we repeat the communication setup against that subaccount.

Concretely, in your Integration Suite subaccount go to Connectivity → Destinations → Download Trust and grab the .pem. It is a self-signed cert whose subject looks like cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/<subaccount-id> with OU=CP Destination Configuration — this is the destination-service signing certificate.

Then, exactly as in the principal propagation post, set up a communication user, a communication system and a communication arrangement (SAP_COM_0008 for Business Partner) in S/4 — but upload this certificate under the communication system's OAuth 2.0 Identity Provider, and copy its subject CN into the Provider Name field.

Note: if the trust is missing or points at the wrong subaccount, the SAML exchange later fails with a very explicit "There is no trust between entities … in client 100". That message contains the subaccount ID it actually saw, which makes it easy to tell that you trusted the wrong one.

Step 2: Create the S/4HANA SAML Bearer destination in the IS subaccount

Next, create an HTTP destination toward S/4HANA in the subaccount where Integration Suite resides. This is the same OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion destination as in the previous post — the MCP server will use it as its target. The important properties:

Name=S4_MCP_GATEWAY_TEST
Type=HTTP
ProxyType=Internet
Authentication=OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
URL=https://my3xxxxx-api.s4hana.cloud.sap
Audience=https://my3xxxxx.s4hana.cloud.sap
Token Service URL=https://my3xxxxx-api.s4hana.cloud.sap/sap/bc/sec/oauth2/token
Client Key / Token Service User=<the comm user from step 1>
authnContextClassRef=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:X509
userIdSource=mail
nameIdFormat=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress

# additional properties
x_user_token.jwks_uri=https://<your-ias-tenant>/oauth2/certs
IntegrationCell.Include=true

Two things that are easy to miss:

  • x_user_token.jwks_uri points at the IAS tenant so the destination service can validate the forwarded end-user token and build the SAML assertion for the real user. Without it, it silently falls back to a technical-user assertion and propagation breaks.
  • IntegrationCell.Include=true is a label on the destination. Without it the destination simply won't appear in the MCP Server wizard's dropdown at all.

Step 3: Build the MCP server in Integration Suite

Now the new part. In Design → Integrations and APIs, create an integration package to hold the artifact.

Inside the package, add an MCP Server artifact. The wizard's first step asks for the source type — pick HTTP Endpoint with OpenAPI Specification:

In the next step, point it at the S4_MCP_GATEWAY_TEST destination with a relative URL of /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER, give it a name and an MCP Path (e.g. /s4_bp_mcp), and leave the runtime profile on Integration Cell:

Skip the AI spec generation. Once the artifact exists, open its MCP Configuration → Source tab and hit Edit API Specification to supply the spec:

Import the OpenAPI/EDMX of the Business Partner service — you can download it from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub, or just pull the live $metadata from your own system:

On the Tools tab, select the operations you want to expose; each one becomes an MCP tool. I started with a single GET A_BusinessPartner → the tool get_A_BusinessPartner. Keep it small; the model routes better with fewer, well-described tools:

The tricky part is the inbound security — this is where the whole principal-propagation story lives. On the Policies tab every MCP server has a mandatory Authentication and Authorization policy, so we look at both.

Authentication

The Authentication policy decides which tokens the gateway trusts. By default an MCP server validates tokens issued through the Integration Suite subaccount's own XSUAA / the IdP configured there. That default path is enough for a client like Joule Work Desktop, which runs its own user-token fetch flow against that trusted authorization server when you add the connector — so the end-user identity is already there, you don't configure anything extra on the gateway.

Our case is different: the token doesn't come from a JWD connector, it's the JWT our A2A agent forwards from Joule, issued by our IAS tenant — and a raw token from that issuer is rejected by the default policy with 401 invalidToken because the gateway doesn't trust it yet.

The fix is to switch the Authentication policy to External OAuth (OIDC) and point it at our IAS tenant. Even though this feels a bit strange — our IAS tenant is treated as an "external" OAuth provider here — the "internal" option is the subaccount's XSUAA, which may well itself be configured to redirect logins to exactly that same IAS. So "external" just means: validate the token directly against the IAS tenant, by its own issuer and keys.

Once External OAuth is selected, there are four fields to fill:

Field Value

Well-Known URLhttps://<ias-tenant>/.well-known/openid-configuration
Audiencethe aud of the token the client actually sends (see the gotcha below)
ClientID Key${authn.oidc.jwt.azp}
UserInfo Key${authn.oidc.jwt.mail}

What these actually do: the Well-Known URL tells the gateway which IAS tenant to trust — it discovers the issuer and the signing keys from there, and validates every incoming token's signature against them. The Audience is the gateway saying "I only accept tokens that were actually meant for this application" — it's matched against the token's aud claim. ClientID Key and UserInfo Key are expressions that tell the gateway which claims carry the calling client's ID (azp) and the end user's identity (mail) — the latter being exactly the identity that gets propagated downstream.

The Audience is the one that'll bite you. Our destination maps userIdSource=mail, and the token that eventually arrives is the one Joule forwarded — i.e. after its app-to-app exchange — so its aud is the Custom Agent App client ID, not the login app you used to get a test token. You find that client ID in your IAS admin console under Applications → your Custom Agent App → Client ID (it's the same value that your agent already validates as its IAS_AUDIENCE). If you set the policy audience to the wrong app, the real Joule token is rejected with 401 invalidToken even though everything else is correct. You can also list multiple audiences comma-separated, or leave it empty to skip audience validation entirely while debugging.

If authentication is not configured correctly, the gateway rejects the call before it ever reaches your backend — a decoded IAS token that doesn't match issuer/audience comes back as:

{ "error": { "code": "invalidToken", "message": "Unable to authenticate user, invalid token" } }

(HTTP 401)

Authorization

The second mandatory policy is Authorization — and this is where it helps to understand how an IAS token is built, because it is fundamentally different from the XSUAA token you may be used to.

An XSUAA access token carries a scope claim (things like myapp.Read, API.invoke), and the default Authorization policy checks exactly that: does the token contain the required scope? An IAS token has no scope claim at all. IAS is an identity provider — it answers "who are you", not "what may you do"; the actual authorization is expected to happen in the target system (the user's S/4 roles, in our case). A decoded IAS user token has mail, sub, azp — but nothing a scope-based policy can match on.

What an IAS token does carry, because it came through Joule's app-to-app exchange, is the ias_apis claim — a list of the exposed APIs the user is allowed to call:

{
  "iss": "https://<ias-tenant>",
  "aud": "<custom-agent-app client id>",
  "azp": "<proxy-app client id>",
  "mail": "felix.bartler@sap.com",
  "ias_apis": ["a2a_custom_agent_app_api"]
}

So the configuration change versus the XSUAA default is: don't check a scope claim, check the ias_apis list instead. Point the Authorization policy's Scope Key at ias_apis and set the expected value to our exposed API:

Authorization field Value

Authorization TypeOAuth Scope OR Developer Key
Scope Keyias_apis
Scopea2a_custom_agent_app_api

The policy then checks whether the ias_apis list contains a2a_custom_agent_app_api — which doubles as a useful access gate: it enforces, right at the gateway, that only users entitled to this agent's exposed API can call it at all.

If authorization is wrong — e.g. the policy still checks scope, which an IAS token doesn't have — the gateway authenticates the user fine but then refuses the operation:

{ "error": { "code": "forbidden", "message": "User doesn't have the authorization to perform this operation" } }

(HTTP 403)

With both policies right, the gateway accepts the real Joule user token, validates it against IAS, reads mail, and forwards the identity to the destination.

Deploy MCP Server

Finally Deploy onto the Integration Cell runtime, and once the Runtime Status reads STARTED the MCP URL is live:

We've basically turned an OData endpoint into a proper MCP Server — with a curated list of tools — and put an auth layer in front of it that enforces principal propagation. Let's test it:

Testing the gateway with curl

Before touching any agent code, it's worth proving the gateway end to end in isolation — exactly like the SAML dry-run in the previous post. MCP over Streamable HTTP is just JSON-RPC over HTTP, so three curl calls do it: initialize (which returns an mcp-session-id response header you must echo back), notifications/initialized, then tools/call.

# USER_JWT = a REAL Joule-forwarded token (see the caveat below), MCP_URL = the deployed MCP server URL

# 1) initialize — grab the mcp-session-id straight from the response header
SID=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%header{mcp-session-id}' -X POST "$MCP_URL" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1.0"}}}')

# 2) say "initialized"
curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST "$MCP_URL" -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}'

# 3) call the tool as the user (note: OData options without `$`, select is an ARRAY)
curl -s -X POST "$MCP_URL" -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_A_BusinessPartner","arguments":{"top":3,"select":["BusinessPartner","BusinessPartnerName"]}}}'

This is the fastest feedback loop for getting the two policies right — the error you get back tells you exactly which stage failed: 401 invalidToken = authentication (issuer/audience), 403 forbidden = authorization (scope/ias_apis), real OData rows = success.

Getting a token that actually works for the test. A plain IAS password grant gives you a token audienced for the login app and without ias_apis, so it fails both audience and authorization — it is not a stand-in for what Joule sends. You have two options to get a realistic token:

  1. Reproduce the app-to-app exchange yourself. This is exactly what Joule does internally: take the user token and exchange it (via the jwt-bearer grant against your IAS, using the proxy app's client credentials and the proxy-to-target dependency) into a token audienced for the Custom Agent App — which then carries ias_apis. If you own the proxy app's credentials, this is the clean, scriptable way and the one I'd recommend for a proper test harness.
  2. Capture a real one. Quicker for a one-off: temporarily log the raw Authorization header in your agent, prompt Joule once, and copy the forwarded JWT out of the logs.

Step 4: The Python agent that calls the MCP gateway

The change on the agent side is small and local: the one place that used to call the destination service and S/4 directly (s4_client.py in the previous post) is replaced by a small MCP client. Everything else — the LangGraph tool, the executor, the IAS middleware on the agent's own inbound endpoint — stays as it was.

The MCP client uses Streamable-HTTP JSON-RPC to call the MCP Gateway. This is part of the standard of MCP - and one could also use a SDK. We do 3 calls: initialize (which hands back an mcp-session-id response header you carry on every following request), notifications/initialized, and tools/call:

# mcp_client.py (abridged)
def call_business_partner_api(user_jwt, top=10, select=None, filter_expr=None, ...):
    session_id = _open_session(user_jwt)        # initialize -> mcp-session-id
    r = requests.post(
        MCP_URL,
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {user_jwt}",   # <-- the whole trick
            "Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream",
            "mcp-session-id": session_id,
        },
        json={
            "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/call",
            "params": {
                "name": "get_A_BusinessPartner",
                "arguments": {"top": top, "select": [...]},   # OData options, no `$`, select is an array
            },
        },
    )
    # tool output comes back as result.content[0].text (JSON string of the OData payload)

The user_jwt it forwards is the exact same token the agent already extracts from the inbound A2A request — unchanged from the previous post:

# agent_executor.py — the token comes straight from the Authorization header Joule sent
auth = context._call_context.state.get("headers", {}).get("authorization", "")
user_jwt = auth[len("bearer "):] if auth.lower().startswith("bearer ") else None
# ... threaded down to the tool, which puts it on the MCP call as Authorization: Bearer

The key point: the agent needs no credentials of its own for the backend. No client secret, no destination binding to S/4 — just the MCP_URL of the deployed gateway. It takes the user's token and passes it on; IAS, the gateway and the destination service do the rest. (The agent's own inbound A2A endpoint is still protected by the IAS middleware exactly as before.)

Two details are worth knowing when calling an Integration-Suite-generated tool: the handshake is session-based (echo the mcp-session-id header after initialize), and the generated tool schema uses OData options without the leading $, with select/expand/orderby as arrays of strings — pass a comma-separated string and the call fails schema validation.

Test in Joule

Deploy the agent, point Joule's agent destination at it, and prompt it — e.g. "show me business partners that start with I". The full chain runs: the agent forwards the user's token to the gateway, the gateway validates it against IAS, propagates the signed-in user through the SAML Bearer destination, and S/4HANA returns exactly the records that user is authorized to see, rendered as a table in the conversation:

This is the point of the whole exercise: the data comes back scoped to the real signed-in user, propagated all the way from Joule to S/4HANA — exactly the behaviour we wanted. And because it now runs through the gateway, we can also see it happen: in Integration Suite under Monitor → Integrations and APIs → Monitor Message Processing (with the Integration Cell runtime selected), each prompt shows up as a BusinessPartnerMCP entry of type MCP Server, status Completed. That's the proof the call actually traversed the MCP gateway rather than some direct backchannel — and the governance, tracing and policy enforcement that come with it apply to every call.

Conclusion

Looks good. We have the full flow in place and can use the MCP Gateway for our A2A Agents. Hope you found this insightful.

The full code is on GitHub under a2a_pp_mcp_gateway/.

This post is part of the Joule A2A series:

  • Connect code-based agents into Joule
  • Secure code-based agents with IAS
  • Handling multi-turn conversations
  • Building custom Joule capabilities: message types in practice
  • Propagate the user identity from Joule into S/4HANA

entry.title: #Demystifying AI Series — Ep 2 # Meet Joule, Why Calling It a "Chatbot" Completely Misses the point
entry.content:
Demystifying AI Series — Episode 2:

"Meet Joule — and Why Calling It a 'Chatbot' Completely Misses the Point"

  You've heard of Joule. You probably filed it under "another AI assistant." Here's why that mental model is the most expensive misunderstanding you can make right now.


The Chatbot Trap

Let me tell you something about chatbots.

We've all used them. The little pop-up in the bottom-right corner that says "Hi! I'm here to help!" and then fails to answer a single useful question.

You type. It responds. You type again. It responds again. Nothing actually happens.

That experience has conditioned most of us to expect exactly nothing from anything called an "AI assistant." Which means when Joule shows up in your SAP system, there's a good chance you dismiss it before you even try it.

I get it. I felt the same way.

But here's the thing — Joule is not a chatbot. And the difference isn't marketing language. It's architecture.

So What Is It, Actually?

Joule is SAP's AI copilot. But that word — copilot — is doing a lot of work.

A chatbot sits outside your system and talks at you.

Joule lives inside your SAP landscape. It knows your data. It understands your processes. It has context about what you're doing, what your business does, and what the next logical step is — because it's connected to the same data that runs your company.

When you ask Joule something in S/4HANA, it doesn't just search the internet. It looks at your purchase orders, your inventory levels, your open approvals. It gives you an answer grounded in your actual business reality.

That's not a chatbot. That's something genuinely different.

And it works across the suite — S/4HANA, SuccessFactors, Ariba, SAP Build, and more. You don't switch tools. You just ask.

When Joule Stops Talking and Starts Doing

Here's where it gets really interesting.

Most people think of AI as something that answers. Joule also acts.

By end of 2025, SAP has 40 Joule Agents running across its portfolio, built on over 2,100 Joule Skills. Let me unpack that for a second.

A Joule Skill  is a specific capability — a trained action. "Retrieve the status of purchase order X." "Draft a job description based on this role profile." "Summarize the key risks in this contract." These aren't responses. They're executions.

A Joule Agent  goes further. It chains those skills together, makes decisions, and works through a task autonomously — with you in the loop at the right moments, not at every step.

Think about what that means in practice.

Instead of navigating five screens to check on an overdue invoice, you ask. Instead of pulling three reports to understand a procurement anomaly, Joule surfaces it. Instead of manually triggering an approval workflow, Joule handles the routing.

The work doesn't disappear. It just stops sitting on your plate by default.

The Part Nobody Explains: Why Joule Actually Knows Your Business

Here's the question most people don't ask: how does Joule know all of this about your company?

The answer is SAP Business Data Cloud.

Think of it as the memory layer. A unified, governed data foundation that connects SAP and non-SAP data — finance, HR, supply chain, procurement — into one coherent picture. When Joule answers a question or executes a task, it's drawing from that picture.

This is what SAP means when they say "relevant, reliable, responsible AI."

Relevant —  because the answers come from your data, not some generic model of the world.

Reliable —  because the data is governed, not a wild west of spreadsheets and exports.

Responsible —  because access controls, compliance rules, and audit trails still apply.

A chatbot has whatever you typed into the chat window. Joule has your business.

What This Means for How You Work

Let me be direct about something.

If you're an SAP professional and you haven't seriously tried Joule yet — now is the time. Not because it's perfect. It's not. But because the professionals who understand its capabilities today will be the ones shaping how it's adopted tomorrow.

Here's what I've noticed: the people who get the most from Joule aren't the ones who use it as a search bar. They're the ones who push it. They ask it to execute, not just explain. They test its limits. They figure out where human judgment is still essential — and where it genuinely isn't.

That critical judgment — knowing when to trust the AI and when to override it — is a skill. And like any skill, it gets sharper with practice.

A Chatbot Answers. Joule Acts. That Distinction Will Define Your Next Few Years.

Calling Joule a chatbot is like calling S/4HANA "a spreadsheet."

Technically you can see the resemblance. Practically, you've completely missed the point.

Joule is not a feature you activate and forget. It's a new way of interacting with enterprise software — one that will become the default interface for SAP systems over the next few years. The professionals who figure that out early won't just work differently. They'll think differently about what their job actually is.

And that, I'd argue, is worth understanding.

 

Your Turn

Have you already seen Joule in your SAP system? What was your first reaction — excited, skeptical, or somewhere in between? Drop a comment — I'm genuinely curious whether the chatbot instinct kicked in, and whether something changed it.

entry.title: SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 + ESM — Unlocking the Power of Spatial Services for Address Validation
entry.content:
Introduction

In today's data-driven business landscape, the quality and accuracy of customer data is a cornerstone of operational excellence. SAP Sales & Service Cloud Version 2 (SSC V2), combined with Enterprise Service Management (ESM), brings a powerful capability to the table: Spatial Services. This feature goes beyond basic CRM functionality — it embeds geospatial intelligence directly into your business processes, starting with one of the most foundational data quality challenges: address validation.

This blog explores what Spatial Services are, how they work within SSC V2 and ESM, and why address validation during Account creation is not just a technical nicety but a critical business enabler.

What Are Spatial Services?

Spatial Services in SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 provide geospatial capabilities that enrich your business data with location intelligence. At their core, they allow your system to:

  • Validate postal addresses against authoritative geospatial data sources
  • Notify users in real time whether an address is verified or unverified
  • Integrate with mapping and data quality platforms such as HERE Maps and SAP Data Quality Management (SAP DQM)

Think of Spatial Services as the geospatial backbone that ensures the data your sales and service teams work with is accurate, complete, and trusted from the moment it enters the system.

The Business Case: Address Validation for Account Creation

Why Address Quality Matters

When a sales representative creates a new Account — whether it's a corporate customer, a partner, or an individual customer — the address they enter becomes the foundation for:

Business ProcessImpact of Bad Address Data
Sales territory managementIncorrect assignments, missed opportunities
Order-to-cash and invoicingFailed deliveries, billing disputes
Field service dispatchingWasted technician time, SLA breaches
Marketing campaignsUndeliverable communications, compliance risks
Compliance & KYCRegulatory failures, audit exposure

A single incorrectly entered address can cascade across multiple downstream processes — creating operational friction, customer dissatisfaction, and avoidable costs.

How Spatial Services Solve This

When Address Validation is enabled in SAP SSC V2 Spatial Services, the moment a user creates or updates an Account, the system:

  1. Captures the address entered in the Account form
  2. Calls the validation engine — either HERE Maps (native integration) or SAP Data Quality Management (if integrated) — to verify the address against real-world geospatial data
  3. Returns a validation status — clearly marking the address as Verified or Not Verified directly on the record
  4. Notifies the user so they can correct the address on the spot, before bad data propagates into the system

This real-time feedback loop transforms address entry from a passive text field into an active data quality gate.

Real-World Business Use Case Walkthrough

Scenario: Onboarding a New B2B Account

Without Spatial Services:

A sales rep types "123 Elm Streeet, Chciago, IL 60601" — two typos, unnoticed. The record is saved. Two weeks later, a product sample shipment fails, a service technician is dispatched to the wrong location, and the territory manager's reporting is skewed.

With Spatial Services + Address Validation enabled:

The same rep enters the address. SSC V2 immediately validates it against HERE Maps. A "Not Verified" indicator appears with a suggestion: "Did you mean 123 Elm Street, Chicago, IL 60601?" The rep corrects it in seconds. The record is saved clean.

The value is immediate, measurable, and permanent — every Account created from that point forward carries trusted address data.

Under the Hood: Two Validation Paths

SAP SSC V2 Spatial Services support two validation modes depending on your landscape:

1. HERE Maps (Default)

When Address Validation is turned on without a DQM integration, HERE Maps is used as the geospatial validation engine. HERE Maps is a globally recognised mapping platform with comprehensive coverage of postal addresses worldwide — making it ideal for multinational sales and service operations.

2. SAP Data Quality Management (SAP DQM)

If your organization has integrated SSC V2 with SAP Data Quality Management, DQM takes over as the validation engine. SAP DQM offers enterprise-grade address cleansing, standardization, and enrichment — particularly valuable for organizations with:

  • High-volume account creation workflows
  • Complex regulatory compliance requirements
  • Existing SAP MDG (Master Data Governance) landscapes

This dual-path architecture gives organizations the flexibility to start with HERE Maps and graduate to SAP DQM as their data governance maturity increases.

Configuration: Getting Spatial Services Running

Setting up Spatial Services in SSC V2 is straightforward and follows a standard administrator workflow.

Step 1 — Configure Users and Access Control

As an administrator, you need to grant the right people access to Spatial Services:

  1. Create a Business Role for users who will work with or administer Spatial Services
  2. Add the Business Service: sap.crm.spatialservice.uiapp.spatial
  3. Enable the Admin App: sap.crm.spatialservice.uiapp.spatialAdmin (service: sap.crm.service.spatialService)

This role-based approach ensures that spatial capabilities are available to the right personas — whether it's a sales operations admin or a data steward — without over-provisioning access.

Step 2 — Enable Address Validation in General Settings

Navigate to:

User Menu → System Settings → All Settings → Spatial Services → General

Turn on the Address Validation switch. Once enabled:

  • Address validation is active for Accounts and Individual Customers
  • HERE Maps begins validating addresses immediately (or SAP DQM, if integrated)
  • The verification status indicator appears on the relevant entity forms

New Account Creation - Validate Address

Existing Account - Validate Address

Individual Customer - Validate Address

Visits - Validate Address and Here Map

Key Benefits for Sales & Service Operations

BenefitDetail
Higher CRM data qualityAddresses are validated at source, not cleaned up later
Better territory managementAccurate geocoding supports precise sales territory assignments
Faster field service dispatchTechnicians are routed to real, verified locations
Reduced invoice and delivery errorsClean addresses mean fewer order and shipment failures
Lower data remediation costsPrevention is cheaper than correction — always
Compliance readinessVerified customer addresses support KYC and regulatory requirements

ESM Perspective: Spatial Services in Service Management

From an Enterprise Service Management standpoint, address validation plays an equally critical role. When service tickets, maintenance plans, or on-site work orders are tied to an Account or Installation Point, the underlying address accuracy directly affects:

  • Service Level Agreement (SLA) adherence — routing delays from bad addresses cause SLA breaches
  • Resource scheduling — field service scheduling engines (like SAP Field Service Management) depend on precise geocoordinates derived from validated addresses
  • Customer experience — a technician arriving at the right place, on time, is the most direct signal of service quality to your customer

Spatial Services bridges the gap between CRM data entry and operational service execution — making it a shared capability that both Sales and Service teams depend on.

What's Next: Growing with Spatial Services

Address validation is the first and most impactful use case, but Spatial Services is designed to grow. As SAP SSC V2 evolves, expect spatial capabilities to extend into:

  • Map-based account and opportunity visualization — see your pipeline on a map
  • Geo-fencing for territory management — dynamically assign accounts based on boundaries
  • Location-aware service routing — optimize field service dispatch using real-time geo data
  • Proximity-based lead scoring — score leads by their proximity to existing high-value accounts

Conclusion

SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2's Spatial Services — and specifically its address validation capability — is a deceptively simple feature with outsized business impact. By catching bad address data at the point of Account creation, organizations protect the integrity of every downstream process that depends on it: shipping, invoicing, field service, territory management, and compliance.

For SAP customers running SSC V2 with ESM, enabling Address Validation via HERE Maps or SAP DQM is one of the highest-ROI configuration steps an administrator can take. It costs minutes to configure and delivers data quality dividends for the entire lifecycle of every Account record in your system.

Clean data in. Better business outcomes out. That's the promise of Spatial Services.

Have questions about configuring Spatial Services in your SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 landscape? Feel free to reach out or drop a comment below.

In your Payroll Schema, do they both exist in the Input Table at their calculated value and at their adjusted value?

Then you could create a first PCR at that point to transfer the values of those WTs into temporary variables (using Operation ADDWT&xxxx), followed by a second PCR that uses 2 constants from V_T511K (one for 15000 and one for 25000) to query the Amounts from these temporary WTs until all options are accounted for.

entry.title: ABAP SQL fine-tune - the training data failed the audit
entry.content:
This post is about the following: Can you teach a small local Model ABAP SQL with training data written by bigger Models, on a budget of 35 Euros and one weekend?
 
I never got as far as the training.

 

The plan

Take a Model small enough to run in Ollama on a Mac mini, and teach it to turn plain-English questions into ABAP SQL. Graded by running the SQL on my A4H system and comparing the rows that come back, not by the SQL text.
 
The setup:
  • Student: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, 4 billion parameters, q8_0 in Ollama,
  • data: the /DMO/ flight reference model on A4H, client 001, 13 Database Tables,
  • grading: each query runs through the ADT data preview, and the result rows are compared with the reference result,
  • budget: 35 Euros, one weekend,
  • success, decided before any training: the fine-tuned Model on its own beats the base Model with a syntax fixer, and not by luck (McNemar test, p < 0.05).

 

Claude Code (Opus 5.5) built everything, OpenAI Codex reviewed.
 

The test set

Rule number one: whoever writes the training data must not write the exam.
 
So OpenAI Codex drafted the questions, every reference query ran on A4H, a second Codex pass answered each question without seeing the first answer, and I reviewed the disputes. 308 questions in the end:
  • 93 easy,
  • 106 medium,
  • 77 hard,
  • 32 the database simply cannot answer (pilot names, weather, that sort of thing).

Frozen, with a fingerprint of the data so nobody could change it behind the scenes.

 
Then the baselines. % of questions answered correctly:
 
Little Qwen out of the box: 14.6%. And most of the misses weren't even wrong logic - 93.5% of his SQL didn't run at all. ABAP SQL wants AS before every table alias, a tilde instead of a dot, and blanks inside the brackets of SUM( ). So Claude wrote a fixer with exactly those three rules, and Qwen jumped to 52.9%. That was the bar to beat. Claude got all 308 right, as one does.

 

Choosing a teacher

The idea of the fine-tune: a big Model writes a few thousand question-and-SQL pairs, we check them, and little Qwen learns from the survivors. But which big Model?
  • Not OpenAI: Codex wrote the test set, and the same family mustn't write the training data,
  • not Claude, Gemini or Grok: their API terms restrict using their output to build other Models (xAI's terms forbid training any AI system on Grok's output, full stop),
  • so an open-weight Model it was.
The teacher: DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MIT licence, and DeepSeek's terms explicitly allow distillation. His checker: GLM-5.2 from Z.ai, a different lab, who answers every question again without seeing the teacher's SQL. Both through OpenRouter, pinned to one provider (DeepInfra), with thinking switched off. The original plan was to rent a GPU on Runpod and host a smaller teacher myself, but OpenRouter was simpler.

 

Every pair had to survive the same obstacle course:
  1. The teacher drafts a question and its SQL.
  2. The SQL runs on A4H and returns rows.
  3. The checker answers the same question blind, and his rows must match.
  4. The question must not be too close to any test question.

 

Plus three gates, written down before the first paid call:
  1. at least 40% of all drafts must survive,
  2. at least 25% of the hard ones,
  3. I audit 50 survivors myself, with at most 2 wrong (at most 1 among the hard ones).
Fail a gate after the one allowed restart, and we stop.

 

Pilot one: DeepSeek + ABAP SQL

A pilot of 300 drafts:
  • 90 easy,
  • 110 medium,
  • 70 hard,
  • 30 unanswerable.

 

DeepSeek wrote them in a few minutes, for 27 cents. Then A4H had its say.
 
Turns out the big Model writes ABAP SQL the way little Qwen does, only with more confidence. FROM /dmo/flight f  without the AS, ROUND(SUM(x), 2) without the blanks ABAP wants, customer~name with no alias called customer anywhere, subqueries in FROM, subtracting one date from another. 57 queries didn't even get an error message, they ended in short DUMPs. In fairness, the dialect notes in his prompt mentioned only the tilde and the column aliases. The rest he was supposed to just know, like Qwen.
 
The checker had his own moment. The prompt told him to answer with sql: null when a question can't be answered. GLM took that literally and sent back the string "sql: null". A4H refused to run it (fair enough), so 28 of the 30 perfectly good unanswerable questions were marked as disputed. That one was on us, not on him.

 

The result: 64 of 300 pairs agreed, and 5 of 70 hard ones. Way under both gates. Pilot one, 29 cents, archived with all its evidence.

 

Pilot two, and one amendment

The one restart we had allowed ourselves came with three changes:
  • a checklist of ABAP SQL rules in both prompts, each rule tested on A4H first, so as not to teach the teacher anything wrong,
  • "set sql to JSON null, not a string" for the checker,
  • Qwen's three-rule syntax fixer applied to both Models' SQL, with the raw SQL kept next to the repaired one, so nothing is hidden.
Much better: 136 of 300 pairs agreed. But only 11 of 70 hard ones, 15.7%, under the 25% bar.
 
Stop.

 

When we looked at why, something odd turned up. The teacher had marked 140 of 180 answerable pairs as "order matters", including questions that never ask for any order. The checker returned the same rows in a different order, and the comparison said no.
 
Fixing that after seeing the failures is exactly the kind of thing that makes a result worthless if you're not careful. My first proposal still let the teacher's flag cast a vote. Codex shot it down: under my rule, he pointed out, not a single order dispute could ever be rescued, so the only way to pass would have been me fixing things by hand in the pilot, and the full run wouldn't do that. Fair.
 
The version that went through:
  • two fresh judgments from DeepSeek and GLM on each question alone - no SQL, no results, no teacher flag,
  • both say "order matters" or both say "it doesn't", or the pair is thrown out,
  • the same rule for the pilot and the full run,
  • disclosed as an amendment made after the failure,
  • and if this fails a gate, the experiment stops, no more fiddling.

 

The two judges agreed on 175 of 180 pairs. Then I labelled 80 pairs of similar-looking training and test questions, which set the threshold for "too close to the test". 25 pairs went out for that. What was left: 132 of 300 pairs (44.0%), and 18 of 70 hard ones (25.7%). Passed. By one hard pair.

 

Then it was my turn

The last gate was me: 50 surviving pairs, 12 of them hard, each with its question, its SQL and its result. Does the SQL answer the question?
42 did. 8 didn't, 5 of them hard. The limit was 2.
 
Seven of the eight added up or compared money in different currencies as if it were one number. Trip fees and flight prices in /DMO/ come in EUR, JPY, SGD and USD. Two pairs summed the booking fees per trip status: for booked trips that is 9,920 EUR + 3,700 JPY + 5,980 SGD + 14,530 USD, which the label proudly reported as 34,130.00. Others compared fees to a cutoff of 50 or 500, or sorted flights into price bands of 300, 1,000 and 1,200, in whatever currency happened to be there. In January 2027 every EUR, JPY and SGD flight already costs at least 1,200, so those carriers came out as entirely "premium". The eighth pair was asked for the average number of flights per carrier, and returned each carrier's flight count without ever computing an average.

 

The worst thing: All eight had run fine on A4H. And for all eight, GLM, from a different lab, answering blind, had written SQL that returned the very same rows. Both Models made the same mistake, so the cross-check waved it through. The teacher prompt even said, in so many words, not to sum or compare amounts across currencies. Two Models agreeing is not the same as two Models being right.

 

So, as agreed before the reassessment, the experiment stops here. No training, no GPU, no little Qwen with a diploma.

 

So was it all for nothing?

Yes.
 
OK, not quite. The automatic checks did their job on syntax: the execution on A4H threw out everything that didn't run, and the cross-check threw out plenty that ran but answered differently. What they couldn't catch was meaning, where both Models were wrong in the same way. 50 pairs read by a human caught that. With a few thousand pairs and no audit, little Qwen would have learned, very diligently, to add yen to dollars.

 

The fine print

In fairness:
  • One teacher and one checker, and both are open-weight. Claude, Gemini, Grok or GPT might have done better, but GPT wrote the test set, and the terms of the other three ruled them out.
  • 50 audited pairs is a small sample, and the labels are mine.
  • The ordering amendment came after we had seen pilot two fail. It's disclosed, it applied to everything, and it got exactly one go.
  • The test set and the baselines stand, and they don't depend on any of this.

 

P.S.: The whole thing cost 64 cents in API calls: 29 for pilot one, 31 for pilot two, 4 for the order judgments. No GPU was rented. Plus Voyage embeddings for the "too close to the test" check. The setup: a Mac mini, A4H in Docker on a VPS, Claude Code (Opus 5.5) doing the building, Codex doing the reviewing. The test set, the code, both failed pilots and every API call are on GitHub: https://github.com/Kamilkov/abap-sql-bench.

entry.title: Email Open Tracking: Why Open Rates Are Unreliable and What Senders Should Do Instead
entry.content:
Introduction

This article explains why email open tracking has become an unreliable measure of subscriber engagement, why this matters for deliverability, and what senders should consider doing to address it.

Email open tracking works by embedding a small invisible image — called a tracking pixel — in each sent email. When the email is opened and the image loads, the send is recorded as an open. Changes in how email clients process these images, particularly since Apple introduced Mail Privacy Protection (MPP) in 2021, have made open rate data increasingly inaccurate and unreliable to use for segmentation decisions.

Why Email Open Rates Are Becoming Less Reliable

Open tracking has always had a known limitation: automated systems — including spam filters, email security gateways, and email preview tools — sometimes load the tracking pixel without a human actually reading the email. These automated loads are referred to as machine opens.

The problem became significantly more widespread after Apple introduced Mail Privacy Protection (MPP) with the iOS 15 update in September 2021. When MPP is active, Apple Mail pre-fetches and caches email content — including tracking pixels — before the recipient opens the message. This means the open is recorded even if the recipient never reads the email. Because Apple Mail and iCloud Mail are used by a large proportion of email recipients, MPP has inflated open rates across the industry.

The Risk of Misclassifying Inactive Contacts

When open rates are unreliable, using them to identify engaged subscribers becomes problematic. Contacts whose emails are auto-opened by Apple Mail or machine processes may appear active in your data when they are not.

This misclassification creates two risks:

  • Inactive contacts continue to receive high-frequency or active-subscriber content, when they should instead receive re-engagement campaigns or be suppressed.
  • Genuinely inactive contacts are mailed too frequently, increasing the likelihood of spam complaints and unsubscribes.

Why Mailing Inactive Contacts Harms Sender Reputation

Mailbox providers — including Gmail, Microsoft Outlook, and Yahoo — use recipient engagement signals to decide how to handle incoming messages. Senders who consistently target inactive recipients are more likely to see their messages filtered to the junk folder or blocked entirely.

This risk increased in early 2024, when Google and Yahoo introduced stricter bulk sender requirements that place additional scrutiny on senders who repeatedly mail inactive contacts. Based on operational monitoring by the Emarsys Deliverability team, senders with large proportions of inactive data are more likely to see declining inbox placement, particularly at Google.

How to Identify Signs of Inactive Data in Your Campaigns

Set Up Google Postmaster Tools

Google Postmaster Tools (GPT) is a free tool provided by Google that shows how Gmail — which typically accounts for 60% or more of most commercial mailing lists — handles your email. It provides trend data and current values for:

  • Sender reputation at domain and Internet Protocol (IP) address level
  • Recipient spam complaints
  • Email domain authentication status

Setting up Google Postmaster Tools (GPT) is strongly recommended for all commercial senders. [Setup steps]

Declining Campaign Performance Indicators

The following patterns in campaign data indicate a potential problem with inactive data:

  • Steady downward trends in opens and clicks — particularly for sends to Gmail recipients since February 2024
  • One domain showing significantly lower click rates than the others
  • A sudden increase in bounces
  • From Google Postmaster Tools (GPT): recipient spam complaints above 0.3%, or domain reputation falling to Medium or Low

What the "Falling Opens, Steady Clicks" Pattern Means

A specific pattern to watch for — most commonly observed in data for Gmail and Microsoft Outlook recipients — is falling open rates alongside steady or stable click rates.

Based on operational monitoring by the Emarsys Deliverability team, this pattern typically indicates that actively-engaged recipients are still receiving emails in their inbox, while messages to inactive recipients are being filtered to the junk folder. The fall in opens is driven by a reduction in machine opens from inactive contacts who are no longer receiving messages in their inbox — not by a genuine drop in readership among active contacts.

This pattern is an early indicator of inbox placement problems and should not be dismissed as a normal open rate trend.

Replacing Open Tracking with More Accurate Engagement Metrics

To build a more accurate picture of subscriber engagement, track the following behaviours instead of, or in addition to, open rates:

  • Link clicks within emails
  • Website or app activity associated with the contact
  • Purchase history

Use these signals to build three engagement segments:

  • Active contacts — recent clicks, purchases, or site activity
  • Inactive purchasers — no recent engagement, but purchase history present
  • Inactive non-purchasers — no recent engagement and no purchase history

These segments allow you to target active users with relevant campaigns, re-engage inactive customers with appropriate content, and suppress or remove long-term inactive contacts with no purchase history.

Managing Contact Frequency and Long-Term Inactive Contacts

Once you have defined engagement segments, apply differentiated sending strategies:

  • Active contacts should receive your full campaign frequency.
  • Inactive contacts should receive fewer campaigns. As the time since last engagement increases, email frequency should decrease.
  • Long-term inactive contacts — particularly those with no purchase history — should be moved to a multi-channel re-engagement programme, or unsubscribed and deleted, depending on their customer lifetime value.

Reducing the proportion of inactive recipients in your sends improves engagement rates and reduces deliverability risk.

Summary

Email open tracking is no longer a reliable indicator of subscriber engagement. Apple Mail Privacy Protection (MPP) and machine opens inflate open rates, making it difficult to accurately identify active and inactive contacts. Relying on open data for segmentation and frequency decisions carries real deliverability risks — particularly following the bulk sender requirements introduced by Google and Yahoo in early 2024.

Senders should consider:

  • Replacing or supplementing open tracking with click behaviour, website activity, and purchase history
  • Segmenting contacts into active, inactive purchaser, and inactive non-purchaser groups
  • Reducing sending frequency to inactive contacts and suppressing long-term inactives
  • Setting up Google Postmaster Tools (GPT) to monitor sender reputation and complaint rates
  • Monitoring per-domain trend data to identify deliverability problems early

These steps improve list health, reduce recipient spam complaints, and protect long-term sender reputation.

entry.title: #Demystifying AI Series — Ep 3:# "You Asked AI. It Answered. But Can You Stake Your Job on It?"
entry.content:
DEMYSTIFYING AI SERIES  ·  EPISODE 03 

 

"You Asked AI. It Answered. But Can You Stake Your Job on It?"

The episode topic owner @petepalme,

💡  AI gives you answers fast. But when you're working in a regulated environment — finance, HR, legal, procurement — fast isn't the same as right. Here's how SAP is trying to solve the trust problem.

The Question That Keeps Coming Up

Here's a scenario most SAP professionals recognize.

You're in a meeting. Someone pulls up a number from an AI assistant. It looks right. It sounds confident. The presentation moves on.

Three days later, someone finds the error.

Maybe it was a rounding issue. Maybe the AI pulled data from the wrong fiscal period. Maybe the logic was fine but the underlying data wasn't governed the way everyone assumed.

The number was wrong. And your name was on the slide.

AI operates at speed. Regulated environments operate at consequence. The question isn't "can AI help?" The question is: how do you know when to trust it?

The Problem With Confident-Sounding Wrong Answers

Here's what makes AI tricky in enterprise settings.

Traditional software fails loudly. A broken query returns an error. A misconfigured report produces blank cells. You know something went wrong.

AI fails quietly. It produces a coherent, well-formatted, confident-sounding answer — and that answer can be wrong. Not obviously wrong. Plausibly wrong. The kind of wrong that gets past the first check.

In a consumer app,  that's annoying.

In procurement,  that's a compliance breach.

In financial reporting,  that's a SOX issue.

In HR,  that's a potential legal exposure.

What the AI sees: a question and a dataset.
What you see: a decision that might get audited.
That gap is the trust problem.

What SAP Built to Close That Gap

SAP's answer has three parts — mapped to what they call "relevant, reliable, responsible AI."

Relevant —  the AI works from your data, not a generic model of the world. SAP Business Data Cloud creates a governed data layer across your SAP landscape so Joule is grounded in the same data your financial close, procurement cycle, and HR processes run on.

Reliable —  the data feeding the AI is trustworthy in the first place. Governance, data quality, defined ownership — these aren't AI features, they're data management fundamentals. But they're what make AI outputs auditable and defensible.

Responsible —  the AI operates within the boundaries your organization has defined — access controls, compliance rules, audit trails. When Joule executes a workflow, there is a log.

These aren't just positioning words. They're architectural decisions SAP made because enterprise customers made it very clear: AI that can't be audited will not be adopted.

What It Still Cannot Solve

Here is where I want to be honest — because this is where AI enthusiasm often goes wrong.

Grounding and governance make AI safer. They don't make AI infallible.

The AI still reasons. And reasoning can go wrong in ways that are hard to catch without domain expertise. An AI with accurate, governed data can still draw the wrong conclusion. It can miss a business rule that isn't codified anywhere. It can apply general logic to a situation that has an exception your team has always handled manually.

The safeguard isn't better AI. It's you.

A well-grounded AI gives you a reliable starting point and a traceable output. What it can't give you is the judgment that comes from knowing your industry, your organization, your specific process — and the three things that went wrong last year that never made it into any system.

That knowledge lives in people. And it's exactly what turns an AI answer into a decision you can stake your name on.

A Different Way to Think About AI Trust

Forget "do I trust AI?" That's the wrong question.

You don't trust a spreadsheet — you verify it. You don't trust a report — you review it. The tool produces output. You apply judgment to that output. AI is no different.

High-stakes, regulated, first-time decisions:  review carefully. Let the AI do the legwork but own the conclusion.

Routine, well-precedented, low-variance tasks:  let the AI run. Spot-check. Move on.

The SAP professionals who navigate this well aren't the ones who blindly trust AI or reflexively distrust it. They're the ones who develop a calibrated instinct for which is which — and build that instinct through practice.

 

Your Turn

In your SAP environment — finance, HR, supply chain, or something else — what's the decision you'd be most reluctant to let AI make autonomously right now?
Drop it in the comments. That answer probably tells you more about your AI adoption frontier than any roadmap will.

⏭  Next episode: SAP BTP's AI Foundation — the engine room that powers everything Joule does, and why it matters even if you never touch it directly.

entry.title: No user exit for that SAP screen? Check who at SAP already enhanced it
entry.content:
This morning a question came in on Q&A: in VA01 and VA02, how do I make the partner function and the partner number read-only on the Partner tab, without modifying LV09CF63? Is there a user exit or a BAdI?

Maybe yes... maybe not. Sandra Rossi had already given the right first step in the thread: read what happens between LOOP WITH CONTROL and ENDLOOP. I did that, and then one more thing that I want to share here, because it works for almost any "is there an exit for this screen?" question.

Step one: search the whole function group, not only the include

The partner tab is screen 1000 of function group V09C. The include from the question, LV09CF63, has FORM SETUP_TC_FIELDS_1000, which does LOOP AT SCREEN and MODIFY SCREEN once per partner line. Nothing to plug into there.

So I searched all 120 includes of V09C on S/4HANA 2023 for the usual suspects: CUSTOMER-FUNCTION, USEREXIT, GET BADI, CALL BADI, ENHANCEMENT-POINT and ENHANCEMENT-SECTION.

Zero classic user exits. One BAdI, BADI_SD_DOC_BP_ADDR_CHECK, but it only decides if the partner address can be changed. And three explicit enhancement points, all in enhancement spot ES_SAPLV09C:

  • IS_ENHANCEMENT_01_01, alone inside PBO module IS_ENHANCEMENT_01 of screen 1000 (include LV09CO01)
  • EHP_LV09CF30_01, in FORM SET_TC_DATA_1000
  • section LV09CF33_01, in FORM USER_COMMAND_1000

The first one looks promising: a PBO module of the screen with nothing in it but an enhancement point. But looking promising is not proof. Does it run once per line, inside the table control loop, or once for the whole screen?

Step two: ask who at SAP already used it

This is the part I like. In ADT, a where-used on include LV09CO01 doesn't only show code. It also lists the enhancement implementations hanging on the program. For V09C there were four, all from SAP:

  • OIG_SAPLV09C_01 (IS-Oil)
  • OIG_LV09CF33_01 (IS-Oil)
  • VPD_SFWS_SC1_V09C_SET_TC_DATA
  • /ACCGO/ACM_EI_TC_DISBL_PARTNER, described as "Enhancement to Disable Partner for Closed Status of Trading Contract"

Read that last description again. SAP's own Agricultural Contract Management needed the same thing the person in the question needed.

To know which point each one implements, table ENHINCINX helps. With PROGRAMNAME = 'SAPLV09C' it returned OIG_SAPLV09C_01 on \PR:SAPLV09C\EX:IS_ENHANCEMENT_01_01. Exactly our point.

Step three: read their code

The IS-Oil implementation has 179 lines, and one block in it is the requirement from the question (I cut the IS-Oil specific condition around it):

loop at screen.
  if ( screen-name = 'GVS_TC_DATA-REC-PARVW' or
       screen-name = 'GVS_TC_DATA-REC-PARTNER' ) and
       gvs_tc_data-rec-parvw <> ' '.
    screen-input = 0.
    modify screen.
  endif.
endloop.

It reads GVS_TC_DATA-REC-PARVW, the partner of the current line, and changes the screen fields of that line. So the module runs inside the loop, once per partner. That answered my "once per line or once per screen" doubt better than any guess, and it came with a template ready to copy.

One more detail from the same code. To know where it is running, the implementation reads data of the calling program with a dynamic ASSIGN: assign ('(SAPMOIGS)T180') to <fs_t180>. The partner screen doesn't know the order header, so if your rule depends on it (for example, only orders created with reference), the same trick gives you '(SAPMV45A)VBAK' in VA01 and VA02. It's not a released interface, and SAP's own code lives with that risk too.

What surprised me most: the answer was not in the include everybody looks at. It was in the where-used list, in objects SAP itself wrote for its industry solutions.

Two things before you code

First, check if you need code at all. SETUP_TC_FIELDS_1000 reads TPAER from the partner determination procedure (VOPA). "No change possible" (AENDB) locks the partner number once it is filled, and "Partner mandatory" (PAPFL) locks the partner function. If your rule is fixed per partner function and order type, customizing already does it. Just not in the standard procedure: in my system 170 order types share procedure TA, so I would copy it to a Z procedure and assign that only to the order type that needs the lock.

Second, what I didn't do. Two of the four implementations came back empty when I tried to read them (the /ACCGO one and the VPD one), and I didn't dig into why. The point and the module are the same in S/4HANA 2025. And I didn't run VA02 with an implementation of my own: if you do, tell me what you see.

If you have your own trick for "is there an exit for this screen?", I would like to hear it in the comments.

entry.title: Best Practices Pipeline for Cloud Integration: Working with Parties
entry.content:
You like to use parties in combination with the Pipeline for Cloud Integration. Parties need to be taken into consideration for different use cases and configuration options. So, this blog post describes how to generally setup your configuration scenarios when using parties.

Note: For exchanging IDoc messages, parties are heavily used when your partner type is not LS. Covering IDocs would exceed the scope of this blog post. For this, I would refer to Enhanced IDoc inbound support for Cloud Integration Pipeline where I describe how to setup IDoc inbound scenarios depending on the sender and (virtual) receiver partner type.

So, let's stick here to the more generic usage of parties. In general, we decided to go for a simplified way how to support parties in the Pipeline for Cloud Integration. We simply combine the party name and  the system name by separating both parts using a period, ".", e.g., PartyA.XYZ. See Scenarios with Sender Party or Receiver Party.

The combined party and system can then be used in different configurations such as:

  • In your alternative partner to determine the partner ID representing the configuration scenario.
  • For sender-specific inbound conversion.
  • In the XSLT to determine the receivers (with party).
  • For P2P, to determine the receiver (with party).
  • For the generic XI/IDoc outbound processing, to define the XI/IDoc connection and scenario settings.

So, here some rules:

  • In your scenario-specific integration flow, maintain the header SAP_Sender as combined sender party and sender system name as described above.
  • For XI inbound scenarios, this is automatically done. Here, the generic XI inbound processing flow creates the header SAP_Sender as a combination of the header SapSenderParty and SapSenderService provided by the XI sender adapter.
  • To determine the configuration scenario, maintain the alternative partner of the partner ID in the Partner Directory accordingly. In this case, define the agency as the combined sender party and sender system name.
  • For receiver parties, maintain the receiver service name in the XSLT to determine the receivers as combined receiver party and receiver system name.
  • For the Point-to-Point pattern, maintain the value of the string parameter receiverDetermination as combined receiver party and receiver system name.
  • For some configuration options, you need to add the combined party name and system name as suffix to the corresponding string parameter.

In message monitoring, you will notice the following:

  • If the header SAP_Sender contains a party, the header SAP_SenderParty is created holding the party name. Furthermore, the value of the header SAP_Sender is split up defining the custom header properties SenderParty and SenderSystem, which are then displayed in the message processing log.
  • If the header SAP_Receiver contains a party, the header SAP_ReceiverParty is created holding the party name. Furthermore, the value of the header SAP_Receiver is split up defining the custom header properties ReceiverParty and ReceiverSystem, which are then displayed in the message processing log.

Let's take a look at some examples.

XI inbound scenario

In this use case, we focus on the inbound side. This is a scenario where we send XI messages to the pipeline whereas the XI header contains both party and system.

We use landscape staging, and would like to test our scenario on the QA landscape. First of all, we need to define a business system alias for the sender system, here BC_02D_S1. In the alternative partner of the alias, we map the actual business system name, here BS_02D_S1Q for the QA landscape, to the alias. We do the same for the second sender, here alias BC_02D_S2 with actual business system name BS_02D_S2Q.

As said, both senders have a party. So, in the alternative partner of the partner ID representing the configuration scenario, we need to define the agency as combination of the party name and the system alias name. In our case BuyerA.BC_02D_S1 and BuyerB.BC_02D_S2, respectively. Scheme of the alternative partner is the sender interface name, ID is the sender interface namespace.

An inbound conversion is needed after the message has been received by the pipeline. In our case, the inbound conversion should be sender-specific. So, for each of the sender we define a string parameter InboundConversionEndpoint with suffix as combined party and sender system alias, here InboundConversionEndpoint_BuyerA.BC_02D_S1 and InboundConversionEndpoint_BuyerB.BC_02D_S2, respectively. As value, we enter the ProcessDirect endpoint of the inbound conversion flows that carry out the conversion.

I switched on the trace for the generic XI inbound processing flow. In the trace, you can see the payload of the incoming message including XI header. So, here you can see that the XI header contains the sender party BuyerA and the sender service BS_02D_S1Q.

In the message monitoring, you can see that the SAP_Sender (Sender in the Properties) is a combination of the party and the business system name, here BuyerA.BS_02D_S1Q. The custom header properties show the sender alias, sender system and sender party information. During runtime, the sender system alias BC_02D_S1 is determined based on the sender business system name BS_02D_S1Q and the landscape stage QA (via the alternative parner of the system alias). The combined party and sender system alias BuyerA.BC_02D_S1 is then used to determine the configuration scenario (via the alternative parner of the configuration scenario). Once, the configuration scenario has been determined, the other parameters are read from the Partner Directory to dynamically define how the message processing behaves.

Configure XI/IDoc Outbound

In this use case, we focus on the outbound side. This is a scenario where we use the generic XI and IDoc outbound processing flows to configure the XI and IDoc receiver adapters and scenario parameters. Here, the receivers contain party.

Again, we use landscape staging. First of all, we need to define a business system alias for the receiver system, here BC_02L_R1. In the alternative partner of the alias, we map the actual business system name, here BS_02L_R1Q for the QA landscape, to the alias.

This is a content-based router pattern. So, we create an XSLT mapping to determine the receivers and upload it to the Binary Parameters of the configuration scenario with ID receiverDetermination.

The XSLT looks as follows. As you can see, we either route a message to the one party or the other. In our case for both parties, the system is the same. However, they can also differ. In our case, the service is defined as combined party and receiver system alias, so either PRTY_02L_Bronze.BC_02L_R1 or PRTY_02L_Copper.BC_02L_R1. Note: in the XSLT we always use the alias, so we can use the same XSLT in each landscape stage.

To configure the XI and IDoc outbound, we support different options: either as message headers in the scenario-specific outbound processing flow, as externalized parameters for dedicated generic XI/Idoc outbound flows, or in the Partner Directory. See XI Receiver Adapter and IDoc Receiver Adapter.

In our case, we use the Partner Directory option. For the Partner Directory option, some of the parameters can be configured for the partner ID representing the configuration scenario or for the partner ID representing the party. In the configuration scenario, you then need to add the combined party and system alias as well as the receiver interface name as suffix to the parameter, e.g., XIAuthenticationType_PRTY_02L_Copper.BC_02L_R1_SI_PurchaseOrderCreatePD_IB_Async. For the parameter InterfaceNameDetermination, it's just the combined party and system alias, e.g., InterfaceNameDetermination_PRTY_02L_Copper.BC_02L_R1.

If you like to maintain party-specific parameters, create a new partner ID with name equals the party name, here PRTY_02L_Copper and PRTY_02L_Bronze. For the parties, you need to add the business system name and not the alias as suffix to the parameter, e.g., XIEndpoint_BS_02L_R1Q.

I switched on the trace for the generic XI outbound processing flow. In the trace, you can see the payload of the outgoing message including XI header. So, here you can see that the XI header contains the receiver party PRTY_02L_Copper and the receiver service BS_02L_R1Q.

To fetch the scenario and connection parameters both are read, the configuration scenario and the party. As you can see, the correct values were read and the message could be successful delivered.

XI/IDoc Outbound without staging

Now, let's check how you could configure XI and IDoc outbound without staging if this is not required. So, we distinguish between two parties but use a business component as receiver system. In this case, you do not need to define a business alias, you simply use the business component name in the configuration, here EDI.

For the party, we also add the business component as suffix to the parameter.

For a complete list of parameters that you can define in both the configuration scenario and the party, refer to XI Receiver Adapter and IDoc Receiver Adapter.
